b816e3b92e02.title: Getting started
b816e3b92e02.content: This page is about the first conversation — what happens between somebody saying “I want to create a folio” and a published site they can open. If you already have a folio and want the toolchain set up, skip to §4 Install and verify. | 1. “Create a folio” is five different requests | 2. How the agent decides — and why it is a table, not a judgement . | The three facts | The seven rules | Why two rules return “ask”, and why that is the point | Changing it | . | 3. What the conversation looks like | 4. Install and verify | 5. Connect your LLM harness | 6. Converting a repository you already have | 7. Seeing it published | 8. Make the landing page yours . | The markdown node you edit | Your own backdrop | Three things it will not do | . | 9. Track the work with beans | Next steps | .

071f4345f921.title: 1. “Create a folio” is five different requests
071f4345f921.content: The agent’s first job is to find out which one you meant. | you mean | you have | what the wrong guess costs you | . | A new folio in a new repository | nothing yet | — | . | folio-assistant added to the repository you already have | your own project, with its own files | a folio scaffolded on top of work nobody looked at first | . | Another folio in a repository that already has one | a folio-assistant layer | a second repository you did not want, and a split corpus | . | A new document inside the folio you already have | a folio, and a chapter in mind | an entire empty folio, and the chapter still unwritten | . | Something you would rather describe in your own words | — | — | . The fourth row is the commonest: asking for a folio when you meant a chapter in one. An agent that scaffolds on it produces an empty repository, not the chapter you asked for.

b31202af4f18.title: 2. How the agent decides — and why it is a table, not a judgement
b31202af4f18.content: The triage is a real, readable artefact rather than a habit an agent might have: . | the process is folio-assistant-core/processes/conduct/getting-started.bpmn; | the decision at its centre is decisions/folio-intent.dmn, a DMN decision table you can open in any DMN tool and change without touching code. | . Source: folio-assistant-core/processes/conduct/getting-started.bpmn — the SVG is generated by bun run cat render:bpmn. The three facts . The gateway reads exactly three things, and two of them come from looking rather than asking: . | fact | how it is obtained | . | isFolio | is there a harness.config.json in this directory? | . | repoHasContent | does the working tree hold files that are somebody’s project, as opposed to being bare? | . | statedIntent | what you actually said — one of the five, or unstated | . statedIntent is a fact about the conversation. It stays unstated until you have said which; it is never inferred from tone or convenience, because that inference is the failure the table exists to prevent. isFolio is about the directory, not about you. Somebody who has used folio-assistant for years is still in an isFolio=false directory when they open a fresh one. Experience changes how much the agent explains; it does not change which branch it takes. The seven rules . | # | said | is a folio | has content | → | . | 1–4 | any of the four | – | – | that branch | . | 5 | unstated | yes | – | ask | . | 6 | unstated | no | yes | ask | . | 7 | unstated | no | no | new folio here | . Hit policy is FIRST, so rules 1–4 come before any inference: a person who says what they want is never overruled by a heuristic about their filesystem. Why two rules return “ask”, and why that is the point . Only rule 7 is decidable by looking. A directory that is already a folio is consistent with three different requests, and a directory with somebody’s project in it is consistent with two, so the table returns ask. ask is an outcome of the table, not a decision the agent reaches. An agent cannot route to a branch the table did not return, so the question is obligatory: an agent left to decide whether to ask will, under pressure to seem helpful, decide not to. When you answer, your answer becomes statedIntent and the same table is evaluated again, which is why the diagram loops back to Read the repository facts rather than jumping straight to a branch: your answer is evidence, read like any other fact. Changing it . The table is an XML file with seven rules in it. To add a sixth kind of request, add a rule and add a matching branch to the gateway — the loader refuses to start a process whose table can return an outcome no branch is named for, so the two cannot drift apart. Nothing in src/ needs to change.

b1b1a92f3c29.title: 3. What the conversation looks like
b1b1a92f3c29.content: The form of the question comes before its content. The agent establishes how you would like to be asked — selectable options, ordinary chat, read aloud, large type — and records it in memory/interaction.json so no future session asks you again. See Accessibility. Then, when the answer is genuinely ambiguous: . You: I want to create a folio . Assistant: This directory already has a folio in it (content/atlas/), so a few things you could mean — . | Add something to the folio that’s here — a chapter, a document (recommended — it is what “create a …” most often means from inside a folio) | Add a second folio alongside atlas | Start a new folio in a new repository | Tell me more | . (No answer is fine — I’ll take 1 and show you before writing anything.) . And then, what to get started on — because “a folio” is not a thing anybody actually wants: . | content type | what it is | needs | . | paper | a scientific paper or book, formal claims backed by Lean, typeset through LaTeX | Lean toolchain, TeX | . | document | structured prose — policy guidance, a standard, a report | pandoc; no Lean, no TeX | . | WHO SMART DAK | a Digital Adaptation Kit (L2) — personas, processes, data elements, decision tables | — | . | WHO SMART IG | a FHIR Implementation Guide (L3), built from an L2 DAK | Java, SUSHI, IG Publisher | . See Content types for what each formalism buys you.

08fe8d61807d.title: 4. Install and verify
08fe8d61807d.content: Follow Installation, then: . bun run cat check-deps . bun should be reported present. Anything your content type needs and does not have is listed with an install hint — a document folio needs none of the Lean or TeX rows.

5e49bfe76f78.title: 5. Connect your LLM harness
5e49bfe76f78.content: Register folio-assistant as an MCP server — see Connecting an LLM harness for Claude Code, Antigravity, Gemini CLI and generic MCP clients. The tools most relevant to this page: . | Tool | Purpose | . | folio_init | Scaffold a folio. Registered as a generic tool, because it runs before the folio has a content type | . | workflow_start / workflow_next / workflow_complete | Run getting-started.bpmn as a real process; workflow_next says what is enabled now and which skill implements it | . | work_plan_prime | Surface the work plan (work items) | . | check_dependencies | Probe which toolchains are installed | . | skill_list / skill_fetch | Discover and load a skill’s instructions | . The full tool list is on the Skills & roles page; content-type tools appear only when the matching adapter is active.

335c654918e8.title: 6. Converting a repository you already have
335c654918e8.content: On the overlay branch the agent looks before it touches anything: . bun run cat scan:repo # read-only report bun run cat scan:repo -- --json # the same, as facts . It sorts what it finds into three buckets — library (source material somebody else wrote), content (prose authored here), and unclassified. unclassified lists what it could not place, for you to decide, because a classifier forced into two buckets has an accuracy nobody can assess and delivers its mistakes as moved files. Then three questions, all answerable by picking, all asked per directory rather than per file: . | Import at all? — everything, sources only, nothing, or pick by bucket. | Where does each group go? — library/ or content/, for the groups it was unsure about. | Leave in place, or reorganise? — leave in place is the recommendation and is meant. Decluttering is a preference; a broken relative link in your README is a defect. | . Nothing moves until question 3 is answered. That step is marked relaxable="false" in the BPMN, so no content package can declare it away. Full discipline: the repo-conversion skill.

11d98e0d092e.title: 7. Seeing it published
11d98e0d092e.content: Creating a folio should end with a link. Immediately after scaffolding: . bun run cat pages:bootstrap # derive the address, report, no probe bun run cat pages:bootstrap -- --wait # probe until the site answers (bounded) . It derives the address from harness.config.json or the origin remote, finds publish workflows by what they do rather than what they are named, and reports one of three things: . |   | means | . | live | the site answered. Here is the link | . | not yet | a measured 404 — the address is right and the first build has not landed there yet | . | could not check | no address could be derived, nothing was probed, or the request failed | . The third is not a softer version of the second: the agent will not tell you “it should be up shortly” on the strength of it, because a measured 404 is evidence and a failed request is the absence of evidence. The same three states are a decision table — decisions/pages-live-gate.dmn — and scripts/pages-bootstrap.ts is tested to agree with it exactly, so the script and the table cannot drift.

b9c132212b5e.title: 8. Make the landing page yours
b9c132212b5e.content: Your site’s home page opens with your layer’s own description, drawn inside your own backdrop. Both come from one file — <name>.json at the repository root — and nothing about the platform’s grumpy cat is written into the template. Change the file; the page follows. The markdown node you edit . // <name>.json -- the DECLARATION. Every key below is one of its top-level // fields, which is what settles this label: it is not the folio config. { "title": "My Folio", // the left sidebar's heading "description": "One line.\nAnother line.", // ← the landing markdown "icon": "mark-small", // which image is the browser tab's "images": [ /* … */ ] } . description is markdown, rendered as-is. It is the node the landing page draws; there is no separate page to keep in step with it, because a description that appears in two places will disagree with itself. Your own backdrop . An image becomes the landing backdrop by declaring role: "landing" and which viewport it is cut for: . { "id": "landing-laptop", "src": "docs/assets/img/my-backdrop.webp", "role": "landing", "layout": "laptop", // also: "mobile", "card" "width": 1671, "height": 941, "textRegion": { "x": 0.205, "y": 0.285, "w": 0.625, "h": 0.235 } } . textRegion is where the words may safely go, as fractions of the image. It is authored, not computed, because it states where the picture is quiet, a judgement about composition that no pixel analysis substitutes for. Render candidate boxes and look at them. Declare one variant per viewport. Each carries its own region, because the same composition sits differently in a portrait crop. Then: . bun run cat docs:harness # push the declaration into docs/_data/ bun run cat docs:harness -- --check # ...and fail if stale (for CI) . Three things it will not do . | you declare | the page does | . | a backdrop with a region | draws your description inside it | . | a backdrop with no region | shows the picture, puts the words below it | . | no backdrop | shows the words alone | . An undeclared region means “do not overlay”, never “anywhere is fine”, because text positioned by guesswork lands on the subject. A folio with no art is ordinary, not broken. If you declare a mobile variant, a phone gets that file; otherwise it gets the widest one you have. That fallback is reported, because the wide crop’s region is wrong for a narrow screen, so a renderer can decline to overlay.

2a7f89183de0.title: 9. Track the work with beans
2a7f89183de0.content: folio-assistant uses beans as the single work-plan mechanism — durable across sessions, shared between agents, committed to the repository. cat-harness-tools/scripts/install-beans.sh # install the CLI if missing beans prime # emit work-plan priming for agents beans list # current open items beans create "draft chapter 1" # open an item bun run cat beans:claim <id> # claim an item . Check before you create. beans create mints a fresh id on every call and dedupes on nothing, so check for an existing item first: re-entering a scripted step without the check floods the store with duplicates. The check is in the todo-manager skill. The SessionStart hook surfaces the plan at the start of every session, and the work_plan_prime MCP tool exposes the same surface to any connected agent.

0f125482624f.title: How it connects
0f125482624f.content: . | Called by: no call activity names this process | Calls: Ask the person, Close the bean, Open the bean | Presented on: no docs page section shows this diagram | Skill: getting-started | Running instances: none recorded | .

1302ae1aa138.title: Lanes — who acts
1302ae1aa138.content: | lane | role | what it does here | . | User (person) | user | Answers the one question Gateway_Intent cannot compute for itself — “ask” is one of five outcomes decisions/folio-intent.dmn can return — and, only on the overlay path, the questions a repo scan cannot answer on its own: which of the content markers it found the harness should declare (Task_ChooseHarnessed), then what to import, where it goes, and who does the importing. | . | Onboarding agent (system) | onboarding-agent | Every write in this diagram belongs to this lane, and each sits behind the non-relaxable read-first gate: nothing is created or scaffolded until Gateway_Intent has classified what was actually asked for. | . | Publish — GitHub Pages | publish-target | Provisions the gh-pages branch before Pages is switched on (Task_ProvisionGhPages), derives the URL, and holds the report that follows it: “unprovisioned” routes back to provisioning, and “live”, “not-yet” and “unknown” are exclusive branches of one DMN-computed gateway, so a failed probe is reported as “unknown”, never as “not-yet”. | .

7d67c3e9243c.title: Steps
7d67c3e9243c.content: Every one of the 16 step(s) is documented. | step | lane | skill / sub-process | what it does | . | Detect the interaction modalityTask_DetectModality | Onboarding agent (system) | interaction-modality | Before the first question is asked, establish HOW to ask it: audio, ordinary chat, selectable options for a user with limited hand function, large-type for low vision. A user who finds the questions unusable never reaches the rest of this diagram. | . | Read the repository factsTask_ReadFacts | Onboarding agent (system) | getting-started | Mechanical, read-only: does the layer’s config (its index.config.json entry; a legacy <name>.config.json only as a fallback) declare a contentType, does the working tree hold somebody’s existing project, and what has the user actually said. These are the three inputs to folio-intent.dmn. Non-relaxable: scaffolding without looking first is how a folio gets written over somebody’s project. | . | Choose from the offered optionsTask_AskIntent | User (person) | interaction-modalitygetting-started | The question is presented as a short list of selectable options, never as free prose, and the list names the top-level content types the agent knows about. The answer becomes the statedIntent fact and the table is evaluated again — the user’s answer is read as evidence, like any other fact. | . | Scan the repo for content worth importingTask_ScanRepo | Onboarding agent (system) | repo-conversiondocument-intake | Read-only. Classifies candidates into library/ (external source) and content/ (authored here), and reports what it could not classify as its own bucket rather than forcing every file into one of the two. Its fourth section, markers, lists the content markers it found — sushi-config.yaml, a legacy dak.json, .bpmn processes, a beans store, library/, Lean, folio manifests — each with its paths, whether index.config.json already declares it (declared, not-declared, or unknown), and the snippet that would. bun run cat-harness-tools/scripts/scan-repo-content.ts --json, a plain command any agent host can run. | . | Choose what the harness readsTask_ChooseHarnessed | User (person) | calls Ask the personrepo-conversioninteraction-modality | A PERSON’S STEP: the scan’s markers that are not yet declared are offered as selectable options — one per marker, each with its paths and what declaring it means, plus “none of these” — and the person picks which parts of the repository to load into the KG. A tap card where the host has one; otherwise a numbered pick-list with a stated default. Never a typed reply. The default declares NOTHING. Only the picks reach Task_Scaffold, which declares exactly those in index.config.json. With no undeclared marker found, nothing is asked. The same question is put after setup by running the scan with --markers (repo-conversion §2a). | . | Import what, where, and who does itTask_ConfirmImport | User (person) | repo-conversiondispatch-agent | Three questions the scan cannot answer: import these or not; library or content for each group; leave the files where they are or reorganize to declutter. Plus whether to dispatch one ingestion agent or a small swarm. Non-relaxable: nobody’s files are moved or imported on inference. | . | Create the repositoryTask_CreateRepo | Onboarding agent (system) | repo-conversion | Only on the new-repo branch, and only after the user has named it. 7d72ee6fb1b1.title: A sub-graph wants to leave
7d72ee6fb1b1.content: Process_GraphDetanglement · strict · 8 step(s) . Part of a repository wants to leave, for size or a semantic reason: four gated stages measure it out of the graph before anything moves, and an administrator authorises the extraction. THE FOUR STAGES ARE GATES, NOT ADVICE: nothing moves until the stage before it measures zero, and they are drawn because a rule in prose is one an agent under pressure talks itself past. Each gate here is a DECISION TABLE: workflow_complete refuses a hand-supplied outcome at a cat-harness.processes:decision gateway, so the branch is computed from the counts a tool already produced rather than asserted. THE SHARPEST GATE IS Detangled?, AND IT IS SHARP BECAUSE OF ITS RULE ORDER. unassignedEdges &gt; 0 returns unknown BEFORE the cross-edge rule is reached, so a zero cross-edge count over an unjudged corpus cannot be read as a pass: unassigned edges are edges the tool declined to judge, not clean ones. A person can skip that rule; a table cannot. EVERY GATE HAS A THIRD STATE AND NONE OF THEM RENDERS IT AS CLEAN. Declared in place? answers unknown on a declaration that did not parse rather than “not yet”, because one says the work has not started and the other says nobody can tell. Detangled? answers unknown on an incomplete measurement. Both route to End_Unknown, which is a REFUSAL to advance — the process stops rather than proceeding on a guess. DECLARING IS CHEAP AND EXTRACTING IS EXPENSIVE, WHICH IS THE POINT. Stage 1 moves nothing: the sub-graph is declared where it already sits, still inside the repository, still connected. STAGE 2 IS A LOOP, AND THE LOOP IS LOAD-BEARING. Prune, merge, factor, or reclassify returns to Measure rather than to the gate, because an assignment is verified by RE-RUNNING and never by being locally reasonable. The four moves are the only four: the first three are the block-scale rule, and “the classification is wrong” is the fourth the repository scale adds because a module’s layer is in doubt the way a block’s chapter is not. ISOLATION IS NOT ZERO EDGES. A sub-graph with no inbound edges can still carry no declaration, no namespace and no published artefact, and lifting that directory produces a repository that cannot say what it is. bootstrap/ is the demonstrated case and the shape to match. THE EXTRACTION IS A PERSON’S DECISION, AND THE LANE SAYS SO. Authorise the extraction sits in the Administrator lane because an extraction moves durable artefacts out of a repository, and deletion-requires-confirmation is not a courtesy the agent may waive: the agent reports what would move, and waits. The administrator lane is the one whose activities change the substrate every other diagram’s lanes bind to, which is exactly what a repository cut does. i i i i i i i i

ad12a7525e71.title: Guideline Updates
ad12a7525e71.content: Process_GuidelineUpdates · strict · 8 step(s) . Taking up a new version of a guideline, or a changed lower layer, is a re-pin and a review at once. The steward maps the affected layers and re-pins them in dependency order. For each re-pin, the adaptation team compares the old version, the new version and its own adaptations. A change that touches no adaptation or policy merges on the technical path. One that does goes to the adaptation committee, which decides for each adaptation whether to keep, revise or retire it. Revisions are ordinary content changes (Process_ContentChangeReview), and the re-pin merges with them. The loop runs until every layer is current. i i i i i i i i

8f1a6564fb6e.title: A harness’s default rendering
8f1a6564fb6e.content: Process_HarnessRendering · strict · 7 step(s) . Renders a harness layer as its default interface: its left-hand nav and docs on its own theme’s art, and a board of its todos and beans from which a reader reads, reviews and, when a write tool is available, proposes changes into the publication review. The theme art goes behind every docs page. Read-only is the floor. Whether the reader may write is a question about the tools the session has (git-push, github-api, github-connector) and the reader’s permissions, so the gateway reads capabilities and never assumes one write path. A change a reader proposes enters the content change review in folio-assistant-core (content-change-review.bpmn); this process enables that review and does not replace it. i i i i i i i

9f1288ce542b.title: The sentence
9f1288ce542b.content: A harness layer adds schematics to a knowledge graph, builds visualisations for them, and describes the tools to use and manage them. Each clause is a different obligation, and a layer that does one without the others is incomplete rather than minimal: . | clause | what it obliges | where it is declared | . | adds schematics to the KG | declare the directories it scans and each one’s graph typology | <name>.json — directory conventions | . | builds visualisations for it | a declared subgraph a reader cannot see is a subgraph nobody checks | the renderer, per subgraph | . | describes the tools | a Tool is a KG node, not a shell string somebody remembers | tools/ | . Every time a layer names a directory as a subgraph, it needs a visualiser and a documentation entry, and it is a finding if there is no skill and no tool for it. The declaration is cheap to write; the other two are what make it real.

669008f70032.title: The four directories every layer has
669008f70032.content: | directory | what it holds | who writes it | . | docs/ | the documentation pipeline — rendered to gh-pages through just-the-docs | the pipeline, from authored pages | . | library/ | ingested L1 sources | ingestion | . | uploads/ | the incoming queue, before anything is decided about it | a person, or an agent on their behalf | . | folio/ | the active workspace | whoever is working | . folio/ is not docs/. docs/ is what a reader browses after the work is done; folio/ is where the work happens — publishing, managing the process, authoring and reviewing content. A layer with a populated docs/ and an empty folio/ has a published record and no workshop.

3e3e6db372e2.title: The default rendering
3e3e6db372e2.content: A harness layer renders, by default, as one thing with two halves: . | LHS navigation + docs/ — the documentation pipeline, one themed section per layer in dependency order. Collapsed, a section is information about that layer; opened, it shows that layer’s docs navigation and the display subgraphs that layer declares. Attribution follows declaration, so a directory renders under the layer that declared it. | A folio/Miro-like board — for accessing, authoring and reviewing content, with beans/ and todos/ managing the pipeline. | . Both sit on the layer’s own theme’s ground: the theme’s avatar art is the background, the way a shared Miro board has one. Arbitrary art sits behind the text, so scrim contrast is measured over pure black (Theming). It is a readable interface. It is a writable one only where there is a writable datastore — a conditional, not a promise, and read-only is the floor. Layout is chosen, not fixed . A folio page may carry its own theme, but layout defaults to choosing dynamically on display size and usability, best-fit among three: mobile, laptop and square. The same three the theme art is already cropped for: a layout with no crop for it has nothing to render on.

c54f9f9983c9.title: Where the requirement starts — bootstrap is the exception
c54f9f9983c9.content: The minimum cat-harness carries a one-line admission test: . If it produces something a human looks at, it is not the harness. That and “a layer renders by default” both hold because the requirement is a floor that rises, not a rule applied uniformly. | layer | visualiser / workflow visualiser | its own .json / .jsonld | . | bootstrap | exempt — it is the navbar footer | required | . | cat-harness | required | required | . | everything above | required | required | . CatBootstrap is the exception, and what it owes instead is its graph: a layer that cannot emit its own .json/.jsonld has not shown it is a graph. It trades the visualiser for a criterion it cannot fail quietly. The exemption is declared data, not a special case in a checker . bootstrap/bootstrap.json carries a renderExemption — of, reason and owes — and the render check reads it through isExemptFrom rather than testing a layer name: a name literal states a rule true only for the layer somebody remembered, and a vendored or renamed bootstrap would silently reacquire the obligation it was excused from. owes is required by the schema: an exemption with no substitute is a hole, and a list of holes is a silence list. bootstrap’s names the two skills that govern its emission, and a test asserts the files it names exist. The guard against spreading is global. The declaration is local because only the layer knows why; renderExemptionProblems takes every layer in the repository, because “only the bottom layer may claim this” is a fact about the stack that a per-instance check cannot see. A second claimant fails check:instance-render. At most one, not exactly one: a repository that vendors no bootstrap has nothing to exempt, and failing it would make it declare something just to stay green. What it owes lives in bootstrap/skills/, bootstrap’s declared skills subgraph, as bootstrap-graph-emission and bootstrap-graph-publication — performed by bootstrap-tools’ export-graph.ts and typed by its GraphExportSchema. The discipline is a declared skills subgraph rather than code comments, so it is read rather than rediscovered. cat-harness is where the rest begins to apply, because cat-harness supplies the layers above with folio/, and a layer that hands its dependents a folio must render one itself. Concretely: a minimal just-the-docs rendering in cat-harness/folio/ describing what a folio is, and cat-harness/folio-render/ for the renderer. The workflow split has the same shape: bootstrap keeps the bare minimum, cat-harness elaborates.

fd6a7f0b9b82.title: Open, and named rather than guessed
fd6a7f0b9b82.content: Three questions are open, and are not written as if decided, because a guessed answer in a published document is how a wrong one becomes canon. The first two are expensive to get wrong: . | Where does the background live? A theme’s backdrop is a sticky-scoped concept today. Making it the page ground is a different CSS surface — body, or a board element — and probably a different crop set: a sticky’s crop is chosen for a card, and a page is a different aspect entirely. | What is the writable datastore? gh-pages is static. The artifact database, a local server, and a GitHub write path through editor links are three different answers with three different security postures. | Which subgraphs are “display” subgraphs? Every declared graphs entry, or an opt-in subset? | .

84ce4bf62bc9.title: KG-DS is the Knowledge Graph Data Store, and its machine is git
84ce4bf62bc9.content: bootstrap/scenarios/roles.json declares a role with this id. Its machine is a git repository, reached through the git CLI or a forge’s API: it is where a declaration and its graph are READ from and where a new layer’s declaration is WRITTEN to. Like any role played by a mechanical actor, it is a real role whose skills are its contract — what it must do, which a test can hold it to. This is why “writable interface if writable datastore” is a real conditional. Writing means a commit through the CLI or a forge API, which is available to an agent with a checkout and credentials and not to a reader browsing a static gh-pages site. The same page can be readable to everyone and writable only to some, and that is a property of the store rather than of the rendering.

b8c662ec573f.title: The Harness
b8c662ec573f.content: TR… . On this page . | Instantiation — named in the index | How the dependency tree is walked . | Bottom-up, from the bootstrap | Three relations, and they are not interchangeable | The bootstrap is the exception, and the floor rises | . | What harnessing a directory obliges . | coverage.process is DECLARED and is not an obligation | The serialisation is the one obligation a Harness MAY NOT waive | . | Three things the model asks for and the code does not do . | 1. Harness is not yet a node kind | 2. The stub is NOT free of the definition’s name | . | Where the rules live | . This page is generated from docs/source/concepts-harness/ — each section below links to its own source. ✎ Edit QA… TR… . A Harness is what makes a Knowledge Graph usable: it renders the graph, serves an interface over it, and supplies the Skills, Workflows and Tools an Agent works the graph with. The Knowledge Graph says what is true; the Harness is how anybody reaches it. Four words carry this page, and each means one thing only (cat-harness#1138): . | word | means | never means | . | instance | a node of some node kind: a workflow instance, a bean, a document-kind record | a repository | . | Harness | one node kind: something that renders a graph and supplies Skills, Workflows and Tools for it | a repository as such | . | layer | a repository in the stack, declared by its <name>.json and ordered by needs | an instance | . | instantiated harness | a Harness that a layer’s index.config.json names as instantiated there | a layer that is merely mounted | . In WHO SMART content, L1 to L5 are knowledge layers, layers of guideline knowledge. A layer on this page is always a repository, never a knowledge layer. A checkout holds several layers. They stack, bottom to top — bootstrap, then cat-harness, then the content core, then folio-assistant — and each inherits what the ones below it declare. Some layers define a Harness (cat-harness is one); others hold content and instantiate a Harness defined by a layer below them, such as an implementation guide instantiating the Harness of the guide base it builds on. That stacking is the subject of this page, along with the two things a Harness owes anything it takes charge of. The key words MUST, MUST NOT, SHOULD and MAY are used here as RFC 2119 defines them, and only in upper case, per RFC 8174. Where a requirement below is not yet enforced by a gate, this page says so at the requirement, because a conformance statement a reader cannot tell from a description of existing behaviour misleads either way.

12b957fabf7d.title: Instantiation — named in the index
12b957fabf7d.content: ✎ Edit QA… TR… . A Harness is instantiated on a layer when that layer’s index.config.json names it. The index is the one file that says which harnesses are instantiated here, as opposed to which layers are merely mounted for their content: . index.config.json which harnesses are instantiated HERE, and where each layer comes from <stub>.config.json how one instantiated harness is configured <stub>.json what a layer DECLARES — its directories and assets . Three files, three questions, and three filenames: two schemas and two readers behind one spelling is a distinction a reader would have to already know. Not yet what the schema says. Today index.config.json has one list, instances[], and it does double duty: it says where every mounted layer comes from, and every name in it is read as an instantiated harness (instantiatedHarnessNames returns the whole list). So a content layer whose index lists nine layers, itself and bootstrap included, has all nine counted as instantiated harnesses. Splitting the list into the harnesses instantiated here and the layers only mounted is cat-harness#1138 phase P2. A layer with no index.config.json falls back to the older rule: a root <name>.config.json instantiates that harness, and a layer that declares directories but carries no config is a dependency, inherited by whoever depends on it, with no interface of its own. An instantiated Harness MUST own the visualisation published at <baseurl>/<stub>. The stem every published artefact is named with is computed in exactly one place — artefactStub, which returns the declared stub when there is one and the name otherwise — so the site build, the Knowledge Graph export and any future artefact cannot disagree about what a layer is called. The stub is intended to be free of the definition’s name. A Harness defined as folio-assistant should be instantiable as my-folio-assistant.config.json, with the config pointing at the definition, and <baseurl>/my-folio-assistant then live. That is not what the code does today — see the last section. It is stated here because the rest of this page assumes it; a reader who tries it is stopped by a gate, not a schema.

97aa8d761d76.title: How the dependency tree is walked
97aa8d761d76.content: ✎ Edit QA… TR… . Bottom-up, from the bootstrap . The stack is walked from the lowest layer up, and each layer overlays what the ones beneath it declared. A Skill, a Voice or a directory contributed low is visible everywhere above it; one contributed high is visible only there. Where two layers contribute the same name, the root wins — it is resolved last precisely so that it can. The order is declared, not computed, in each layer’s needs array: . { "name": "<content-core>", "needs": ["bootstrap", "cat-harness"] } . It is declared so that no consumer has to hardcode the layer names. needs is OPTIONAL, and an absent value means undetermined rather than needs nothing. [] is a layer asserting it sits on nothing, which is true of exactly one layer here, while absent is nobody having said. A consumer treating absent as [] would place every unlabelled layer on the floor beside the bootstrap. Names are used rather than paths, because a layer is identified by its name everywhere else and a path breaks the moment a directory moves. Three relations, and they are not interchangeable . Between repositories — as opposed to between layers in one checkout — the Knowledge Graph page sets out three relations, and a fourth, associated, needs no order at all. Each has its own carrier here: . | relation | runs | carried by | . | depends | Content → Content | needs — the layer stack, foundation first | . | references | Tool → Content, Test → Content | remoteGraphs — a graph this layer knows about and does not hold | . | utilizes | Tool → Tool, Test → Tool, App → Content | dependencies in the config — what this layer USES, overlaid | . | associated | Content ↔ Content, any harness | associatedHarnesses — a harness this one knows, and where it is published; never loaded or materialized (skill associate-harness) | . Only depends fixes an order, so only depends can have a cycle in it, and a cycle there is a defect rather than a shape. A Tool repository references a Content repository without sitting above or below it; a consumer application utilizes a Content repository it may depend on not at all. That is why a consumer needs all three and collapsing them loses the distinction: “what must be built first”, “what do I know exists”, and “what do I read at run time” are three questions with three answers. The bootstrap is the exception, and the floor rises . bootstrap sits at the bottom and does not render. It is the navigation footer; what it owes instead is its own .json and .jsonld — “that is its existence”. The rendering obligation is a floor that rises: it starts at cat-harness, which is obliged because it supplies the layers above it with folio/. A layer below that floor declares its exemption in renderExemption rather than being silently excused, so the exemption is a statement somebody made and not a gap somebody left.

eda72f297822.title: What harnessing a directory obliges
eda72f297822.content: ✎ Edit QA… TR… . A Harness does not only hold directories. It harnesses them — and a datastore such as a git repository is harnessed the same way, through Tools: the Harness names the Skills that reach the store, and a Tool supplies the mechanism. That indirection is what lets the same Harness be driven against a different store without rewriting a Skill. Declaring a directory is a promise. It says this layer holds a graph of that kind and a consumer may scan it, and the obligations below are what make the promise keepable. They are stated in full by harness-requirements and measured by check:subgraph-coverage. | obligation | declared as | the question it answers | . | serialisations | coverage.serialisations | is each node addressable as json, jsonld and schema.json? | . | visualiser | coverage.visualiser | can a person LOOK at this? | . | docs | coverage.docs | can a person READ ABOUT this? | . | skill | coverage.skill | is an agent handed something that GOVERNS this? | . The first four are per declared directory. A fifth, a starting README, is per layer and is ranked harder still: without one a reader cannot enter the layer. coverage.process is DECLARED and is not an obligation . A directory may also name the BPMN process that governs it — coverage.process, a diagram’s basename such as document-ingestion. The generated subgraph README then draws that diagram, links its .bpmn source and lists the subprocesses it calls, so the page a reader lands on says how the directory is worked rather than only what is in it. It sits apart from the four above in two ways. It is not owed. Most directories are not the subject of a process, so an absent coverage.process means NOT DECLARED and never “no process” — the same third state readOnly keeps — and a directory declaring none gets no such section and is not a finding. What is a finding, ranked major, is a declared name that resolves to no diagram: somebody said, and what they said points at nothing. There is no exempt.process: declaring nothing already says it. It is declared rather than inferred from a diagram’s event names. An event’s name is editorial text, so rewording it would silently unlink the page, and a diagram touches several directories while being about one — document-ingestion reads uploads/ and writes library/. The serialisation is the one obligation a Harness MAY NOT waive . A Harness MUST serve json, jsonld and schema.json at a harnessed directory’s own URL and at every node beneath it, and MUST NOT be excused it. coverage.exempt carries three keys — visualiser, docs, skill — and deliberately not a fourth, and the coverage check ranks a missing serialisation as an unmet obligation with no by-kind test at all. bootstrap is excused a visualiser because its json and jsonld are its existence, so the serialisation cannot itself be excusable, or the exemption would excuse everything. The visualiser is the courtesy; the serialisation is the existence claim. A Harness SHOULD provide a visualisation, and which kinds owe one is a question about the kind rather than a blanket rule: an active state directory in the repository root — beans/, todos/, fsh-guts/ — owes one because a Harness renders something for each state directory it initialises, while a kind that was never going to need one is not carrying a debt. That difference is why the coverage axis ranks findings major and minor rather than counting them: major is an obligation this kind owes and the layer has not met; minor is nobody having said yet, for a kind that never owed one. A single count would rank beans/ having no viewer alongside a kind that never needed one. A Harness SHOULD also carry a docs/ directory documenting itself, and every Harness SHOULD have one. cat-harness renders its own through the plain documentation path — no extensions, no JavaScript where it can be avoided — which is why it is the one layer that owns a renderable kind at all: a layer owns the kinds it can render.

377b7933c9b4.title: Three things the model asks for and the code does not do
377b7933c9b4.content: ✎ Edit QA… TR… . Two parts of the model above are intended and not implemented. Each says what a reader will actually hit, because a page that described them as working would send somebody to look for code that is not there. 1. Harness is not yet a node kind . Harness is intended to be one node kind, and an instantiated harness an instance of it (cat-harness#1138 phase P2). Nothing in the schemas registers that kind today: a layer declares a name, directories, assets and needs, and what makes it a Harness rather than a dependency is the presence of a config file, which is a fact about the filesystem rather than a declared type. Without a kind there is nowhere to say what a Harness of a given sort MUST supply, so every obligation on this page is prose rather than something a declaration can be validated against. 2. The stub is NOT free of the definition’s name . The model says a Harness defined as folio-assistant MAY be instantiated as my-folio-assistant.config.json, with the config pointing at the definition. Three places refuse it, and they refuse it consistently: . | instanceConfigFilename composes the filename from the declared name, so the stub is derived rather than chosen. | The left-hand navigation tests for <declared name>.config.json when deciding whether a harness is instantiated on a layer — a differently-named config would leave the layer with no tile. | check:instance-config reports a config whose filename does not match its layer’s name as a finding, reading it as a rename half-done. | . And the config carries no field pointing at a definition, so even were the filename freed there is nothing for it to point with. Freeing the stub means adding that pointer first; the filename rule is the symptom. Neither item blocks the other. Instantiation works, the dependency walk works, and all four coverage obligations are carried and checked. What is missing is the part that would let a Harness be validated as a Harness rather than recognised as one.

ad13957e3856.title: Where the rules live
ad13957e3856.content: ✎ Edit QA… TR… . As with every page here: the discipline is in the Skills, and where a Skill and this page disagree, the Skill wins and this page is wrong. | question | where it is answered | . | What the Knowledge Graph is, and which way its references run | The Knowledge Graph | . | How a layer declares its directories, and every graph typology | directory-conventions | . | What a visualiser owes a declared directory | Subgraph viewers | . | What a Skill states and what a Tool supplies | skills-and-tools | . | Why a tile belongs to the Harness rather than to a node | harness-tiles | . | Context Overlays, and how an Agent’s conditions are set | Managing agent context | . The declaration schema, including needs, remoteGraphs, renderExemption and coverage, is schemas/cat-harness.ts; the config schema, including dependencies, is schemas/harness-config.ts.

507df1063a4b.title: 1 — Human and agentic actors and the SMART Guidelines content levels
507df1063a4b.content: ✎ Edit QA… TR… . WHO envisions a future where everyone in the world benefits fully and immediately from clinical, public health and data-use recommendations. SMART Guidelines systematize and accelerate the consistent application of recommended, life-saving interventions in the digital age. | level |   | what it produces | on the slide | . | L1 Narrative | WHO guideline publications | a knowledge graph of literature and data sources | | . | L2 Operational | the Digital Adaptation Kit | structured requirements | | . | L3 Machine readable | FHIR implementation guides | fully computable assets | | . | L4 Executable | reference software | customizable software | | . | L5 Dynamic | trained, optimised algorithms | advanced analytics for precision health | | . What spans which levels. Under the five levels the slide draws four bars, and each bar’s reach is part of what the slide says. Read from the slide’s geometry, not its text: . Bars under the SMART levels on slide 1: each cell spans the levels its bar covers. | bar | L1 | L2 | L3 | L4 | L5 | . | content | content: L1 to L3 | | | . | test data | | test data: L2 to L4 | | . | tooling | | | tooling: L3 and L4 | | . | apps | | | | apps: L4 | | . No bar reaches L5. Two questions sit at the two ends of the band. How can I reliably author, review and adjudicate faster? is drawn on the left, over L1, beside the human actor (the cat at the laptop). How am I verifiable? is drawn on the right, over L5, beside the agentic actor (the robot cat). The slide pairs each question with an actor by position only; it states no pairing in words. Sources: WHO SMART content types — the five layers; the DAK layer’s library/mehl-2021-who-smart-guidelines (the primary source, Lancet Digital Health 2021); the DAK layer’s library/9789240093362-eng §1.2 (WHO’s handbook restating them).

0d510d82025c.title: 2 — Accessing the WHO L1 corpus
0d510d82025c.content: ✎ Edit QA… TR… . WHO’s public-health information is split between literature repositories, IRIS (DSpace), and structured indicators in the World Health Data Hub. Unifying them into one knowledge graph needs a platform with room to grow to about 10 TB, with high throughput and without high network costs. | problem | proposed answer | . | Egress fees make serving 10 TB globally unpredictable | a zero-egress public CDN holding signed static assets | . | Automated traffic, above all in emergencies, can overload internal systems | decouple: an internal secure origin, published snapshots outside it | . | Authenticity and chain of custody in an era of AI-generated content | sign every published asset (WHO Trust Network gateway) | . The architecture drawn on the slide runs in three stages. An internal secure origin (IRIS and the Data Hub) feeds an automated compile engine: folio-assistant builds, signs, snapshots and publishes. That engine feeds a public CDN, named on the slide as Cloudflare R2 storage and the Cloudflare edge network. Sources: kg-to-portal (package and per-asset signatures; “a CDN is a LAYER”); large-datasets (the WHO IRIS source descriptor); the IRIS replica (the DSpace skill). Misaligned — proposal, not decision: the repository treats the CDN as a swappable layer. kg-to-portal and large-datasets’ artifact store name Cloudflare and R2 only as examples beside GitHub Pages, jsDelivr and S3. The slide names Cloudflare as the choice. The 10 TB figure, the World Health Data Hub and “Swiss Observatory schemas” appear nowhere else in the repository. The choice is proposed, with no outcome yet, between three options (Cloudflare R2 + CDN, GitHub Pages alone, another object store + CDN), and what has to be measured comes before one is chosen. Read this slide as that proposal.

d8454095b0fd.title: 3 — The ten components of an L2 DAK
d8454095b0fd.content: ✎ Edit QA… TR… . | # | component | what it holds | . | 1 | Health interventions and recommendations | the WHO guideline’s recommendations; informs DAK scope | . | 2 | Generic personas | roles, responsibilities and interventions of the targeted personas | . | 3 | User scenarios | brief narratives of how the personas engage with the system | . | 4 | Business processes and workflows | generic clinical and non-clinical workflows; when data is collected and used | . | 5 | Core data elements | data for decisions and indicators; informs forms and L3 interoperability | . | 6 | Decision-support logic | decision tables for counselling and treatment algorithms | . | 7 | Scheduling logic | decision tables for scheduling by care plan (formerly part of 6) | . | 8 | Indicators and monitoring | numerators and denominators; person-centred data linked to aggregate | . | 9 | Functional and non-functional requirements | key functions and requirements of a digital tracking and decision-support system | . | 10 | Test scenarios | test data and scenarios to check a system against the other nine | . The slide drew nine cards and put the tenth, testing: test data and test harness, beside them. The squares below give all ten a card, and are generated from DAK_COMPONENTS (the DAK layer’s scripts/gen-dak-components-figure.ts), so a component added there cannot go without one. The figure as it appeared on the slide (2026-09-30): nine cards . Sources: DAK_COMPONENTS (ten: the original eight plus scheduling logic and test scenarios); the SMART Base 1.0.0 DAK logical model; the L2 artefacts and their skills. Misaligned, in three directions: the speaker notes said 8. The figure shows 9 cards, with testing beside them. The SMART Base DAK logical model (DAK.fsh) declares 9 fields: test scenarios in, scheduling logic carried inside decision-support logic. This repository’s DAK_COMPONENTS counts 10 and marks scheduling logic as not yet formalized. WHO’s IG starter kit disagrees with itself the same way: its introduction counts 9 with scheduling and no testing, and its table counts 9 with test scenarios and scheduling inside decision support. Scheduling logic is authored as DMN decision tables but may not yet be formalized as its own L2 component or L3 artefact, and that is the gap the logical model shows. The notes are corrected in the owner’s copy.

10f9dff6f8ab.title: 4 — Existing L1/L2/L3 schemas
10f9dff6f8ab.content: ✎ Edit QA… TR… . SMART Base publishes a JSON Schema, and an OpenAPI description, for every DAK logical model and value set. Examples are the decision-support logic, health interventions, functional and non-functional requirements, program indicator, core data element, persona and business-process workflow models, the Dublin Core metadata set, and value sets such as the classification of digital health interventions. A source reference such as DecisionSupportLogicSource must give exactly one of url, canonical or an inline instance. . On the slide the JSON Schema is drawn over the list as a callout of one entry, DecisionSupportLogicSource, so it reads as “this is what one of these entries holds”. The QR code beside it points at the API page. Source: https://smart.who.int/base/dak-api.html; the artefact index in the DAK layer’s fhir-artifact-index, built at publish from the IG’s source. Aligned in count, not checked item by item: the slide shows “Logical Model Schemas (25 available)”. 3b071aa4daf9.title: 6 — Roles, tasks, skills and tests in the publication lifecycle
3b071aa4daf9.content: ✎ Edit QA… TR… . An agent uses skills to execute one or more tasks in a process. It works with a knowledge graph of static context (skills, user stories) and dynamic context. The diagram as it appeared on the slide (2026-09-30) . How the slide labels the diagram. On the slide the terms sit around the BPMN picture and lines tie each one to a part of it: . | Process points at the whole diagram, captioned (publication lifecycle), with (Context) beside it. | User Story is tied to Role, and Role to one lane, the one labelled Editor (editors and authoring agents). | Task points at one node in that lane, Edit Doc (today: editing and HCI validation). | Skill hangs off that task, and Test hangs off the skill. | The work items icon sits by agentic state and the sticky note by human state. | . So the slide says a user story names a role, a role is a lane, a task is a node in it, a skill belongs to a task, and a test belongs to a skill. ee5e24976f90.title: 7 — BPMN execution, from deterministic to agentic
ee5e24976f90.content: ✎ Edit QA… TR… . BPMN execution skill: given a process, context, state and role, use one or more skills to execute a task. | Deterministic end: managed agent execution of a single task. The tool is any open-source BPMN engine, and state and swimlanes are strictly enforced. | Agentic end: agents work across most or all tasks. The tool is an agentic swarm with ungoverned state. Agents “relax” swimlanes, and mechanical plus agentic QA/QC reports mitigate it. | . What the two halves place where. On the deterministic side the human and the agentic actor stand beside the flat diagram’s lanes, with one sticky note on the authoring task and one work item on the test task: one task at a time, each state marker where its task is. On the agentic side the human rides above the board, a row of agents hangs beneath it, and work items lie in every lane. 6c538a5dc35e.title: Asking a person, in one reusable way
6c538a5dc35e.content: Skill human-agent-discussion: Ask a person (or a sibling agent) for what no file holds. First determine where you are — the context, the Role you act as and theirs, the Process and task (or that you are idle) — and ask about whichever you cannot determine before anything else. Then context, the options, a recommendation and what happens with no answer, then ONE question. Named by: Complete initialization, Determine the harness and repositories, Human–agent discussion, Initialize a harness . You are the agent that needs something only a person can supply: a choice, a judgement, or a step only they have the rights to perform. Every diagram in bootstrap that needs one calls processes/human-agent-discussion.bpmn as a call activity rather than drawing its own asking.

ad28c4744a9c.title: Before you ask: determine where you are
ad28c4744a9c.content: The diagram’s first three tasks come before any question, and each is declared as a precondition of the first one (bootstrap.processes:precondition … before="A_GiveContext"): . | determine | what you must be able to say | why it comes first | . | the context (A_DetermineContext) | what is already known, each fact with where it came from; which declaration governs it (the layer’s <name>.json, the diagram you are in, the Skill its task names); and whether the question has already been decided — earlier in the conversation, or in a declaration that quotes the person’s ruling | a settled question asked again reopens a decision and spends the person’s attention twice. Cite what you read, not what you remember | . | the Roles (A_DetermineRoles) | which Role you are acting as — the lane of the task that called this discussion — and which Role the person you ask holds | an Actor performs a task in a Process as a Role; nothing is a Role by nature. Who holds the decision decides whom you may ask: only the Requestor chooses a harness | . | the Process and task (A_DetermineProcess) | the Process, the lane and the task the question belongs to — “Process: Initialize a harness, at Determine the harness and repositories, as the Bootstrapping Agent” — or that you are in none: you are idle, classifying a request to find the Process it belongs to | a reader who does not know which Process you are in assumes the last one’s rules still hold | . Say all three in the message, as the first part of the context. A caller that already determined them hands them in; you check them rather than re-derive them. You are out of process — the Process is undetermined — when you cannot name it, when two candidates fit, when the step you believed was next is not the one the diagram enables, or when the work in hand is not what you said you would do. Do not infer your way back in. What cannot be determined is asked first . When any of the three cannot be determined, that becomes the first question of this same discussion (A_AskUndeterminedFirst), and the caller’s question waits, counted. Ask about the outermost first — the Process, then the Role, then the context — since the outer answer usually settles the inner. It goes through the same order as every question below, and it allows no default: a Process or a Role assumed rather than confirmed is an authority nobody gave you. Its answer is recorded, the three are determined again, and only then is the caller’s question put. If it is declined or met with silence, record what is still open and stop: a step completed in the wrong Process records an authority that was never given. I am in Initialize a harness, at Determine the harness and repositories, acting as the Bootstrapping Agent. I cannot tell whether you are the person who wants this repository set up, or relaying for someone: the request came from another agent’s message. If you are, I will ask you which harness next; if not, I will stop and record that the Requestor is unknown, since only the Requestor chooses. Are you the person who wants it set up? (One more question after this one.) .

b926b0435606.title: The order is the rule
b926b0435606.content: . | Context. Where you are (the three determinations above), what is being decided, what depends on it, and what you already know, each fact with where it came from. In the message itself: a link is where somebody goes for more, never where the terms are defined. | Options. Every option still open after you narrowed from context, each with what it costs and what it makes hard to undo. An option you could have ruled out yourself wastes the reader’s attention. | Recommendation. The option you would take, marked, and why. | What happens with no answer. Said before the question, so silence has a meaning both sides agreed to before it happened: the default, when the caller allows one, or “the question stays open and the work stops”. | One question, answerable by picking. With several decisions open, ask one in full and give a count for the rest. | . The test before you send it: can the reader answer without opening anything? If not, the question is not ready.

ea4629a921ad.title: What can come back, and where each ends
ea4629a921ad.content: | what came back | what you do | end | . | an answer that settles it | record it, and who gave it (a person or an agent) | Answered — or, when it answered a question about where you are, determine again and put the caller’s question | . | an answer that does not settle it (a kind instead of an option; two options) | follow up once, narrower, naming what is still open | back to the answer | . | a refusal | record what was asked and what is still open | Still open | . | nothing | apply the default only if the caller allows one, and say so; otherwise record what is still open | Default applied or Still open | . A default is the caller’s to allow, never yours. A caller allows one only when the decision is reversible and its own instructions name the default. It is recorded as assumed, with the default named, never as the person’s answer, and the next message tells them it was applied so they can reverse it. Which harness a repository becomes allows none: a wrong answer does not fail, it succeeds at being the wrong thing (confirm-harness).

d856a1418f1e.title: The record
d856a1418f1e.content: In the form the caller asks for. For bootstrap’s harness question that is a document conforming to discussion.output.schema.json (discussion). For a step only the person can perform (complete-initialization), it is the step with the person’s word beside it. A person saying “done” is recorded as their word, and the next check decides whether it holds.

85ad8c1381d4.title: Symmetric in its participants
85ad8c1381d4.content: The answering lane is a person or a sibling agent that already holds the answer. The record says which, because the two are evidence of different weight. Neither is refused, and they are not conflated.

ebc775d2549e.title: Human Translation Workflow
ebc775d2549e.content: Process_HumanTranslation · advisory · 16 step(s) . The human half of translation: a coordinator assigns a locale to a qualified translator, the translator works in their own tool, a subject-matter expert judges accuracy, and only then is the result official. You are in this process when a person is doing the translating. translation-workflow is the machine half — extraction, injection, staleness — and it hands off to this one at exactly the point a judgement is needed. The two are separate because completeness is mechanical and accuracy is not: the coordinator’s gate asks whether enough strings are filled, the reviewer’s asks whether they are right, and no amount of the first substitutes for the second. What makes a translation OFFICIAL is the reviewer’s sign-off, never the file being complete. i i i i i i i i i i i i i i i i

f5d8aa3fef76.title: Steps
f5d8aa3fef76.content: Every one of the 16 step(s) is documented. | step | lane | skill / sub-process | what it does | . | Identify content and target localeTask_IdentifyContent | Translation Coordinator | translation-manager | The coordinator selects:- Which content nodes need translation (block, section, chapter, or folio)- The target locale (one of the supportedLocales in <name>.config.json)- The priority and deadline | . | Assign to qualified human translatorTask_AssignTranslator | Translation Coordinator | translation-manager | The coordinator assigns the translation to a qualifiedtranslator, ideally a domain SME for the content area. For WHO content,the translator should be familiar with WHO SMART Guidelines terminology.The assignment includes:- The .pot file(s) from extraction- The domain glossary- Context notes (block kind, chapter, content area)- The deadline | . | Check translation completenessTask_CheckCompleteness | Translation Coordinator | translation-manager | Verify that all msgid entries have msgstr translations.Partial translations are acceptable for initial submissions but must beflagged for follow-up. The coordinator checks:- % of strings translated- Any fuzzy-flagged entries- Missing critical sections | . | Request completion of remaining stringsTask_RequestMoreWork | Translation Coordinator | translation-manager | Return to the translator with a list of untranslatedor fuzzy strings that need attention. | . | Receive assignment and materialsTask_ReceiveAssignment | Human Translator | translation-managertranslation-managertranslation-manager | The translator receives:- .pot file with source strings (msgid)- Domain glossary with approved term translations- Context notes per string- Style guide and WHO terminology referencesTools: Poedit, Weblate, Crowdin, or direct .po editing. | . | Translate strings in preferred toolTask_TranslateInTool | Human Translator | translation-manager | The translator works through each msgid, producingmsgstr translations. They:- Follow the domain glossary for technical terms- Preserve placeholder tokens ({1}, {2}) in position- Mark uncertain translations as #fuzzy- Note any source ambiguities for the coordinator | . | Submit completed .po fileTask_SubmitPO | Human Translator | translation-managertranslation-managertranslation-manager | The translator submits the completed .po file backto the pipeline. This may happen via:- Git commit + push- Weblate/Crowdin sync- File upload to the coordinator | . | Review translation for accuracyTask_SMEReview | Subject-Matter Expert / Reviewer | translation-managertranslation-managertranslation-manager | A subject-matter expert reviews the injected translatedmarkdown for:- Clinical/technical accuracy of terminology- Preservation of meaning from the source- Cultural appropriateness for the target locale- Consistency with the domain glossaryFor WHO content: the SME verifies that normative statements(“SHALL”, “SHOULD”, “MAY”) are translated with the correctforce in the target language. | . | Return for correction with annotationsTask_ReturnForCorrection | Subject-Matter Expert / Reviewer | translation-manager | The reviewer annotates specific passages that needcorrection and returns to the translator with detailed feedback.Each annotation includes:- The passage in question- What is wrong (terminology, meaning, style)- The suggested correction or reference | . | Sign off translation as officialTask_Signoff | Subject-Matter Expert / Reviewer | translation-manager | The reviewer signs off the translation, making itofficial. This records:- signedOffBy: the reviewer’s identity- signedOffAt: the current timestamp- sourceHash: SHA-256 of the source .md- level: block | section | chapter | folioTool: translation_signoff MCP tool | . | Extract the POTTask_ExtractPOT | Automated Pipeline | shared step GT_ExtractPottranslation-manager | Scan the source content and write the translatable strings to .pot files at the configured granularity: segment prose by paragraph, shield what must not be translated (math, code, labels, Lean companions) as placeholders, normalise whitespace, and extract metadata such as titles, alt text and captions. Tool: the translation_extract MCP tool. | . | Prepare domain glossaryTask_PrepareGlossary | Automated Pipeline | translation-manager | Builds the locale term base for the target locale from the layered glossaries, has it reviewed, and hands it to the translator with the POT. Each layer’s glossary is the directory it declares with the glossary graph typology. Precedence, within one subject area (the scheme’s subject): the more authoritative (lower) layer fixes a term’s translation; a layer only adds, and may not give a fixed term a second translation. A match in another subject area is a sense check for the reviewer, not a violation. Previous translations of related content are evidence for a term with no fixed form, not a source that overrides one. A fixed translation is an authored term with a non-empty, non-fuzzy msgstr in its scheme’s catalogue (translation-manager, “The locale term base”). | . | Inject the POTask_InjectPO | Automated Pipeline | shared step GT_InjectPotranslation-manager | Read the .po file and the source .md, substitute msgstr for msgid, unshield the placeholders, and write the translated .md to translations/<locale>/. Check structure (paragraph count, heading levels) and completeness (no empty msgstr), and lint (doubled punctuation, orphaned placeholders). Tool: the translation_inject MCP tool. | . | Round-trip translation QATask_RoundTripQA | Automated Pipeline | shared step GT_RoundTripQatranslation-manager | Back-translate the target-language .md into the source language and compare the meaning with the original. It catches semantic drift and terminology misses that a forward-only fluency check cannot see, and tells the two apart. Tool: the translation_validate MCP tool.No gateway follows: drift or clean, the translation goes to Task_SMEReview with the findings attached. Which of two readings is right is a human call (translation-manager, “route drift to a human reviewer”), and every translation in this workflow is reviewed and signed off anyway, so a clean result is evidence for the reviewer and never a way around them. The findings include translation:glossary:check’s: every glossary term translated against the locale term base, fixed before sign-off, with its glossary section in the KG QA report. | . | Append WHO disclaimer (if DAK)Task_AppendDisclaimer | Automated Pipeline | translation-manager | For WHO SMART Guidelines content, automatically appendsthe WHO legal disclaimer:- Translation not created by WHO- English edition is authoritative original- WHO not responsible for translation accuracyOnly applies when folio contentType includes WHO/DAK content. | . | Write status.json (official)Task_WriteStatus | Automated Pipeline | shared step GT_WriteTranslationStatus (official = true)translation-manager | Record the translation’s standing in translations/<locale>/status.json. The official input says which: false records it as unofficial ({ official: false, generatedBy, generatedAt }), usable but shown with a warning badge; true records the human sign-off with the SHA-256 of the source .md, so a later change to the source marks it stale. | .

8ab6817d8789.doc: An IG site, built from the AST on its cache branch
8ab6817d8789.title: An IG site, built from the AST on its cache branch
8ab6817d8789.content: Process_IgAstCache · advisory · 6 step(s) . How an IG repository’s own site is published, and how the AST it is built from is kept current (skill ig-build-pipeline §”The AST cache lifecycle”). THE RULE. An IG site is built from the IG Publisher AST read from the IG repository’s cache branch cat/fhir-harness/fhir-ast/<package id>, never from Publisher HTML. The publish refuses an AST that is not valid for the commit it publishes (ig-cache.sh restore then verify). A later commit that changes no IG input (sushi-config.yaml, ig.ini, input/) does not make the AST stale. THE REFRESH. The cache is written by ONE thing: fhir-harness’s reusable workflow .github/workflows/ig-ast-refresh.yml, which an IG repository’s Site publish calls as its first job (ast; template templates/ig-repo-site/site-publish.yml). It runs the Publisher through the AST exporter on a GitHub runner (Java, 10 GB heap, tx.fhir.org). It seeds the branch only from a commit on the default branch whose inputs equal the tip’s. A valid AST is a cache, not a release: every page drawn from it carries the provisional mark (ig-ast-delta). i i i i i i

43e1bacaf031.doc: An IG site, built from the AST on its cache branch
43e1bacaf031.title: Steps
43e1bacaf031.content: Every one of the 6 step(s) is documented. | step | lane | skill / sub-process | what it does | . | Restore and judge the cached ASTTask_Restore | Site build (agent, stage-local) | ig-ast-deltaig-build-pipeline | ig-cache.sh restore --ig-root . fetches cat/fhir-harness/fhir-ast/<package id> into output-ast/ (with the Publisher’s txcache/), then ig-cache.sh verify runs ig-ast.ts validity: exit 0 valid, 1 stale-inputs (naming which input), 2 cannot-tell. A restore that finds no branch is a miss, judged as not valid. In an IG repository’s site route this is the first pre step, ig-site:ast (ig-repo-site.ts ast). | . | Build and publish the site from the ASTTask_BuildSite | Site build (agent, stage-local) | ig-render-jekyllig-build-pipeline | Runs the site route’s steps via stage-local.ts → build-instance-site.ts: ig-site:sidecars (IG API sidecars, if the landing layer has the step), ig-site:compose (artefact index and thin pages from the AST, the IG composed at the root), ig-site:openapi (if the IG holds OpenAPI pages), ig-site:publisher-pages (the AST’s resources as <Type>-<id>.json at the root, the build stamp), and last ig-site:bar (the IG’s slim bar on pages written after publisher-pages). Published at the root from the default branch, as a preview otherwise. When the restore recorded the cache commit, the site reads the AST from that commit by raw URL rather than copying it: the artefact pages draw each full resource there, the IG API sidecars are read from its ig-api/ (fhir-harness#344), and the artefact index from its fhir-artifact-index/index.json, which the site points at with fhir-artifact-index/index.ref.json instead of serving (#358). The root <Type>-<id>.json copies are then reduced (minified, no narrative, no ELM data; #359), and the JSON-LD graph (artifact/*.jsonld) names each root file first and the cache copy as its mirror. The full resources are the cache commit’s and the release’s package.tgz. | . | Review the site’s sizeTask_SizeReview | Site build (agent, stage-local) | ig-publication | Read the size report the build printed before its push, and fix what it shows, or raise a decision card with the owner when no known fix applies (skill ig-publication §”Size review”). The report is cat-harness-tools site-size.ts (bun run cat site:size), written as site-size.json beside the build, never into the site. It gives the total against the published gh-pages root, the top directories, the size by extension, the biggest files, byte-identical duplicates, source maps, the directories named after another layer of index.lock.json, and the directories the shared-assets host could serve. Growth over the budget (10% or 10 MB) is a warning. The review is advisory and never refuses a publish. | . | Dispatch AST refreshTask_Dispatch | Publication manager (owner, or the agent the owner delegates to) | ig-build-pipeline | Actions → “IG AST refresh (by hand)” → Run workflow on the default branch, inputs ref = the default branch, force = false. Set force = true only to rebuild a cache that is valid but suspected wrong. | . | Build the IG with the AST exporterTask_Export | AST refresh (GitHub runner: IG Publisher with the AST exporter) | ig-publisher-fork | The runner mounts the layers the IG repository’s index.lock.json pins, then restores and judges the cache itself. When it is not valid (or force is set) it rebuilds with the Publisher fork (Tool ig-ast-export, litlfred/fhir-ig-publisher at the pinned claude/ast-export commit). A stale cache is first rebuilt incrementally (IncrementalBuildCli), falling back to a full AstExportCli build with -tx; a force run, a pre-export caller, or a missing or cannot-tell cache always builds in full, and a release needs a full build. The caller’s optional pre-export overlay command runs before a full build; the inputs it changed are put back and the AST is recorded against the clean commit’s input digest (ig-ast.ts source-inputs). The AST just built must itself be valid for the commit, or the run fails. | . | Seed the cache branchTask_Seed | AST refresh (GitHub runner: IG Publisher with the AST exporter) | compiled-artefact-cache | ig-cache.sh seed --ig-root . --push: one commit holding the AST, the Publisher’s expansions and txcache/, the IG API generated over that AST (ig-api/, ig-api-cache.ts) and the artefact index built from that tree (fhir-artifact-index/index.json, ig-index-cache.ts), which the site reads by raw URL; its subject recording the package, counts, Publisher version and source commit. Refused when the candidate is under 90% of the incumbent’s resources or edges (the no-shrink gate). | .

28da5eba366d.doc: Is the incremental IG AST what a full build would have produced?
28da5eba366d.title: Is the incremental IG AST what a full build would have produced?
28da5eba366d.content: Process_IgAstDeltaReview · advisory · 4 step(s) . The review step of an incremental FHIR IG build, as its own subprocess: list and inspect the differences between the incremental IG AST and what a full build would have produced, then accept them or raise a finding. WHERE IT SITS. In ig-incremental-build.bpmn it belongs between Task_Merge and Task_Qa: after the restored and rebuilt records are merged, before the QC gates read the aggregate. That diagram does not call it yet; ig-ast-delta §”Where this sits in a process” states the placement. WHAT IT GUARDS. An incremental build rebuilds only the cone of a change, computed on the BASE edges. If the cone rules miss a coupling, a resource that should have changed does not, and nothing downstream can tell: the merged AST looks exactly like a correct one. So a person reads the delta, and a difference nobody can explain is treated as a missed coupling. WHAT IT DOES NOT CLAIM. A clean review says the delta is explained, not that the IG is correct. The AST stays a cache: every rendered page carries the provisional mark, and a release is still cut from a full build (ig-publisher-reduction P4). i i i i

244bb5fac201.title: Each IG, composed into a host docs site and rendered with just-the-docs
244bb5fac201.content: Process_IgDocsSiteCompose · advisory · 4 step(s) . How a host docs site builds every IG it mounts INSIDE itself, so each IG’s pages wear the host’s chrome (one sidebar, one search, one language selector) rather than being a site of their own. Subprocess of Tool stage-ig-sites; reached from docs-site-publish’s Call_InstanceSites (skill docs-generation). NO IG PUBLISHER RUNS. build-ig-site turns the IG’s source into Jekyll source, with the Publisher’s site.data.fhir filled from the IG’s AST and sushi-config.yaml, and the host’s ONE Jekyll build renders it with just-the-docs (skill ig-render-jekyll). Which IGs is DATA: each instance whose fhir-artifact-index/menu.json records a source.of (the IG repository) and source.ref (the commit). No workflow and no step here names an IG. feature-staging.yml runs the same steps for a pull request’s preview, with --changed-files, so only the IGs a change reaches are rebuilt. An IG repository building its OWN site runs stage-ig-sites --only <instance> --source <checkout> --compose-into <shell> --compose-at-root, which is ig-ast-cache’s Task_BuildSite, not this process. i i i i

aebd9d909364.title: Incremental IG build
aebd9d909364.content: Process_IgIncremental · advisory · 19 step(s) . An incremental build for a FHIR Implementation Guide: compile, validate and re-render only the dependency cone of a change, then gate on QA and deploy. One change (a PR push or a push to main) runs: restore the derived state, compute the change’s dependency cone, compile and validate only the cone against the warm validator, re-render the cone’s records, rebuild the meta-index, assemble the site, gate on QA, then deploy; on main or a release only, seed the cache from the green build. An unusable cache falls back to a full build; an environment error stops the run and logs why. Advisory, like the other content-type pipelines: the package that owns the content owns what adequate means. i i i i i i i i i i i i i i i i i i i
