db014de185bc.doc: Assessment of open standards for requirements and methodologies fitting the bootstrap Requirement
db014de185bc.title: Assessment of open standards for requirements and bootstrap mapping
db014de185bc.content: Status: evaluated and recommended, NOT adopted into bootstrap. Issue #1164. Owner, 2026-09-23, choosing markdown front matter for requirement documents: “1 for now. need bean to assess open stds for requirements/methodologies that fit in”. The bootstrap Requirement (bootstrap/schemas/requirement.schema.json) is deliberately free of outside concepts. This methodology assesses open standards across three categories — interchange formats, statement templates & grammars, and quality models — evaluating their licensing, governance, serialization overhead, and exact field-by-field fit to the bootstrap Requirement. It concludes with concrete architectural recommendations on layer placement and verifies the no-outside-concept boundary.

8a94bce2abaa.doc: Assessment of open standards for requirements and methodologies fitting the bootstrap Requirement
8a94bce2abaa.title: 1. The bootstrap baseline: the six parts of a requirement
8a94bce2abaa.content: In the bootstrap and harness architecture, a requirement is defined by six essential parts (formalized in Issue #2405, FR-007/FR-008, and documented in skills/content/requirements-planning/requirement-definition.md): . | Identifier (id): A globally unique URI/slug (req:<slug>), with each individual requirement statement addressable as req:<slug>#<key> and each success criterion addressable as req:<slug>#<key>/<criterion>. | Title & Label: A concise human-readable heading (title for the document, label for each atomic statement). | Statement & Conformance (requirement, conformance): Exactly one sentence that a reviewer or test can say yes or no to, qualified by an RFC 2119 conformance verb (SHALL, SHOULD, MAY, SHALL NOT). | Rationale / Benefit (benefit, description): The justification explaining why the obligation exists and what value it delivers. | Parent & Lineage (derivedFrom): Direct upstream references in the specialization/conformance lattice. | Acceptance & Verification (successCriteria[]): At least one concrete success criterion (criterion) with an explicit verification method (verification ∈ {test, inspection, review, analysis}). A requirement without a success criterion can be filed and never judged. | . A requirement document is authored in Markdown with YAML front matter or stored as JSON, and grouped into a RequirementSet (reqset:<slug>) tracking stages (draft → proposed → approved → planned → in-progress → delivered → accepted), member decisions, work plans (work items), and recorded human sign-off attestations.

676dc79dc256.doc: Assessment of open standards for requirements and methodologies fitting the bootstrap Requirement
676dc79dc256.title: 2. Survey of open standards
676dc79dc256.content: Category A: Interchange formats . 1. ReqIF (OMG Requirements Interchange Format v1.2) . | Origin & Governance: Object Management Group (OMG formal/2013-10-01), originally standardized by ProSTEP iViP. Also ISO/IEC 17506:2022. | Licence: Open specification, royalty-free (RF). | Maturity: High. De facto interchange standard in automotive, aerospace, and defense systems engineering (supported by IBM DOORS / DOORS Next, PTC Integrity, Siemens Polarion, Dassault, Eclipse ProR). | Serialization Overhead: Very high. XML-based schema with extensive metamodel indirection: REQ-IF → CORE-CONTENT → DATATYPES → SPEC-TYPES (SpecObjectType, SpecRelationType) → SPEC-OBJECTS → SPEC-RELATIONS → SPECIFICATIONS (SpecHierarchy). Attributes require multi-level XML wrappers (<ATTRIBUTE-VALUE-STRING>, <THE-VALUE>). Line-based Git diffs of raw ReqIF XML are unreadable. | Semantic Alignment to Bootstrap: . | SpecObject maps to a bootstrap Statement (or an atomic Requirement). | SpecObjectType defines attribute metadata. | ReqIF.Name maps to title / label. | ReqIF.Text maps to requirement (statement text). | SpecRelation (type derives or parent) maps to derivedFrom. | Verification items can be modelled either as separate SpecObjects linked via SpecRelation (type verifiedBy), or as structured attributes on the SpecObject (VerificationMethod, SuccessCriteria). | . | Verdict: Excellent for enterprise import/export projection; totally unsuitable for native storage or authoring in Git. | . 2. OSLC-RM (OASIS OSLC Requirements Management v2.1 / OSLC Core 3.0) . | Origin & Governance: OASIS Open Standard. | Licence: OASIS Royalty-Free (RF) on Limited Terms. | Maturity: High in ALM/PLM linked-data ecosystems (IBM Engineering Lifecycle Management, Siemens, Eclipse Lyo). | Serialization Overhead: Moderate to High. RDF graph representations (JSON-LD, Turtle, RDF/XML). Relies on URI dereferencing, Linked Data Platform (LDP) protocols, and ontology vocabularies (oslc_rm:, dcterms:). | Semantic Alignment to Bootstrap: . | oslc_rm:Requirement resource type. | dcterms:identifier maps to id / key. | dcterms:title maps to title / label. | dcterms:description maps to requirement statement text. | oslc_rm:derivedFrom and oslc_rm:elaboratedBy map to derivedFrom / dependsOn. | oslc_rm:validatedBy links to test artifacts or verification definitions. | . | Verdict: Natural fit with knowledge-graph / JSON-LD export pipelines (ns.jsonld, kg-export), but introduces unnecessary REST/graph server assumptions if forced into the local authoring loop. | . Category B: Statement templates and grammars . 3. EARS (Easy Approach to Requirements Syntax) . | Origin & Governance: Alistair Mavin, Philip Wilkinson, Adrian Harwood, Mark Novak (Rolls-Royce plc / IEEE International Requirements Engineering Conference 2009). | Licence: Unencumbered, open methodology. | Maturity: High. Widely adopted across aerospace, automotive, medical device, and agile systems engineering. | Serialization Overhead: Zero. Operates directly on the requirement statement natural language text. | The Five EARS Patterns: . | Ubiquitous: “The <system> shall <system response>.” . | Example: “The harness SHALL validate every block against its declared schema.” | . | Event-driven: “When <trigger>, the <system> shall <system response>.” . | Example: “When a plan is requested, the agent SHALL produce a requirements document and work plan.” | . | State-driven: “While <in a state>, the <system> shall <system response>.” . | Example: “While the requirement set is in draft stage, the tool SHALL allow modification of statement keys.” | . | Unwanted behavior: “If <trigger/error>, then the <system> shall <system response>.” . | Example: “If a statement lacks success criteria, then check:requirements SHALL emit a validation finding.” | . | Optional features: “Where <feature is present>, the <system> shall <system response>.” . | Example: “Where LaTeX tooling is installed, the adapter SHALL generate typeset math blocks.” (Complex requirements combine While, Where, When, and If clauses). | . | . | Semantic Alignment to Bootstrap: . | Fits directly inside the requirement string in bootstrap Statement. | The <system> noun maps to actors / harness components. | Conformance verbs align 1:1 with RFC 2119 / bootstrap SHALL, SHOULD, etc. | Can be validated deterministically by regular expressions or syntax AST checkers in check:requirements without altering the data schema. | . | Verdict: The optimal statement syntax pattern for authoring requirements in the harness. | . 4. ISO/IEC/IEEE 29148:2018 (Systems and software engineering — Requirements engineering) . | Origin & Governance: Joint ISO/IEC/IEEE standard. Replaced and consolidated IEEE 830, IEEE 1220, and IEEE 1233. | Licence: Formal international standard (copyright held by ISO/IEEE; concepts open for reference). | Maturity: Definitive international benchmark for requirements engineering. | Serialization Overhead: Zero (process and semantic standard, not a file format). | Core Elements: . | Requirement Construct (Clause 5.2.4): Defines standard syntax comprising Conditions, Subject, Conformance Verb (“shall”, “should”, “may”), Action/Object, and Constraints. | Verification Methods (Clause 6.4): Explicitly standardizes the four fundamental verification methods: . | Test: Quantitative verification using automated or manual test cases with controlled inputs and measured outputs. | Inspection: Visual or manual verification by examining the product, code, or documentation without executing it. | Analysis: Verification using mathematical models, calculations, simulations, or formal logic proofs. | Demonstration: Qualitative verification of observable operation under specified scenarios (analogous to review). | . | . | Semantic Alignment to Bootstrap: . | Bootstrap’s verification method enum (test, inspection, review, analysis) is an exact 1:1 realization of ISO 29148’s verification quartet (with review representing demonstration/adjudication). | Traceability relations (derivedFrom, dependsOn) align with Clause 5.2.7. | . | Verdict: The conceptual foundation for the harness’s requirement definition. | . 5. IEEE Std 830-1998 (Software Requirements Specifications — SRS) . | Origin & Governance: IEEE Computer Society. | Status: Officially withdrawn and superseded by ISO/IEC/IEEE 29148:2011/2018. | Licence: Historical IEEE standard. | Maturity: Historic benchmark, but obsolete in modern systems engineering. | Fit to Bootstrap: Premised on large, monolithic, document-centric Software Requirements Specification (SRS) manuals (Section 1 Introduction, Section 2 General Description, Section 3 Specific Requirements). Bootstrap requirements are atomic, graph-linked statement nodes in Git rather than monolithic text chapters. | Verdict: Superseded. Retained only for historical traceability; all modern harness mappings should cite ISO/IEC/IEEE 29148:2018. | . Category C: Quality models . 6. ISO/IEC 25010:2011 / 2023 (Systems and software Quality Requirements and Evaluation — SQRE) . | Origin & Governance: ISO/IEC JTC 1/SC 7. | Licence: Formal international standard. | Maturity: Universal international taxonomy for software quality characteristics and Non-Functional Requirements (NFRs). | Structure: Defines 8 product quality characteristics (expanded to 9 in 2023): . | Functional Suitability (completeness, correctness, appropriateness). | Performance Efficiency (time behaviour, resource utilization, capacity). | Compatibility (co-existence, interoperability). | Interaction Capability / Usability (recognisability, learnability, operability, aesthetics). | Reliability (maturity, availability, fault tolerance, recoverability). | Security (confidentiality, integrity, non-repudiation, accountability, authenticity). | Maintainability (modularity, reusability, analysability, modifiability, testability). | Portability (adaptability, installability, replaceability). | Safety (2023 addition: operational risk, hazard mitigation). | . | Semantic Alignment to Bootstrap: . | Bootstrap Statement differentiates kind: "functional" and kind: "non-functional". | For kind: "non-functional", bootstrap requires a category string. | ISO/IEC 25010 characteristics provide the canonical controlled vocabulary for this category field (e.g. security, performance-efficiency, maintainability, reliability). | . | Verdict: Strongly recommended as the controlled taxonomy for non-functional requirement validation in cat-harness. | . 7. INCOSE Guide for Writing Requirements (INCOSE-TP-2010-006-04, 2023) . | Origin & Governance: International Council on Systems Engineering (INCOSE). | Licence: INCOSE copyright; educational / professional guidance. | Maturity: Universal de facto standard for requirements authoring quality and automated linting rules. | Structure: Defines 9 Requirement Characteristics (Necessary, Appropriate, Conforming, Singular, Feasible, Verifiable, Correct, Conforming, Complete) and 40+ specific quality rules: . | Singularity: One requirement per statement; no compound sentences with “and/or”. | Verifiability: Must state conditions that can be definitively verified. | No ambiguous words: Avoid vague terms (“user-friendly”, “rapid”, “cost-effective”, “easy”, “robust”). | No escape clauses: Avoid “where possible”, “as appropriate”, “to the extent practical”. | Active voice: Clear subject acting upon an object. | . | Semantic Alignment to Bootstrap: . | Directly justifies the bootstrap requirement rule: “one sentence a reviewer can say yes or no to” and “at least one success criterion with a verification method”. | Provides the precise linting rules for automated QA criteria in check:requirements. | . | Verdict: Strongly recommended as the rule basis for requirements quality linters. | .

879246f0f35d.doc: Assessment of open standards for requirements and methodologies fitting the bootstrap Requirement
879246f0f35d.title: 4. Architectural assessment: complexity, cost, and layer placement
879246f0f35d.content: Why nothing is adopted into bootstrap (the no-outside-concept rule) . Bootstrap (bootstrap/) is the foundational, zero-dependency substrate of the entire folio-assistant platform. It defines the core data contracts and schemas that every tool, harness, and workspace inherits. | No External Dependencies: Bootstrap cannot import or depend on heavy XML parsers (for ReqIF), RDF/triple-store engines (for OSLC), or specialized NLP libraries. | Git Hygiene and Line-Oriented Diffs: Markdown front matter (.md) and lean JSON files (.json) produce readable, clean Git diffs on PR reviews. ReqIF XML produces massive, unreadable multi-thousand-line diffs for minor attribute changes. | Speed and Portability: Validating bootstrap schemas via Zod is nearly instantaneous in Bun or Node. It introduces zero runtime overhead. | Conclusion: Any standard mapping or projection must live in higher layers (cat-harness, or a content layer above it). Injecting outside formats into bootstrap would violate the repository’s foundational architecture. | . Architectural layer placement . The diagram below illustrates the strict separation of concerns across layers: . ┌────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐ │ Layer 2: Projection & Integration Adapters (tools / folio-assistant) │ │ - ReqIF Exporter/Importer (.reqif XML for DOORS, Polarion, Cameo) │ │ - OSLC-RM Linked Data Provider (JSON-LD / RDF / LDP) │ └──────────────────────────────────┬─────────────────────────────────────┘ │ maps to/from ┌──────────────────────────────────▼─────────────────────────────────────┐ │ Layer 1: Harness Validation & Quality Linters (cat-harness) │ │ - EARS Pattern Validator (checks statement regex / grammar in CI) │ │ - INCOSE Requirements Linter (flags vague words, compound sentences) │ │ - ISO 25010 NFR Category Checker (validates non-functional categories)│ │ - check:requirements gate & requirement-set adjudication │ └──────────────────────────────────┬─────────────────────────────────────┘ │ validates ┌──────────────────────────────────▼─────────────────────────────────────┐ │ Layer 0: Bootstrap Substrate (bootstrap/) │ │ - Pure Markdown Front Matter + Zod Schema │ │ - Zero outside concepts, zero external dependencies │ │ - 6-part requirement structure: id, title, statement, conformance, │ │ derivedFrom, successCriteria (test, inspection, review, analysis) │ └────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘ .

200607ae0827.doc: Assessment of open standards for requirements and methodologies fitting the bootstrap Requirement
200607ae0827.title: 5. Concrete recommendations
200607ae0827.content: . | Maintain Markdown Front Matter + Zod as Native Format: . | The current Markdown front matter format for requirement documents (and JSON for programmatic requirement nodes) is optimal. | It is human-readable, machine-checkable via strict Zod schemas, and perfectly suited for Git pull request workflows. | Do not replace the front matter format with ReqIF XML or raw OSLC RDF. | . | Implement EARS Grammar Verification in cat-harness: . | Add an EARS pattern checker into check:requirements (or as a dedicated script scripts/check-ears-patterns.ts). | Every requirement statement should be checked against the 5 EARS patterns (Ubiquitous, Event-driven, State-driven, Unwanted behavior, Optional features). | This provides immediate authoring feedback and enforces rigorous syntax without changing the underlying data schema. | . | Standardize NFR Categories on ISO/IEC 25010: . | In cat-harness validators, enforce that for statements with kind: "non-functional", the category field belongs to the ISO/IEC 25010 quality taxonomy (security, performance-efficiency, compatibility, interaction-capability, reliability, maintainability, portability, safety). | . | Build Projection Adapters in Higher Layers on Demand: . | When interoperability with enterprise requirements tools is required: . | Develop tools/reqif-adapter: converts RequirementSet and Requirement nodes into standard OMG ReqIF 1.2 XML packages and vice versa. | Develop tools/oslc-rm-adapter: exposes requirement graphs via OSLC-RM JSON-LD contexts mapped through ns.jsonld. | . | Keep these tools isolated from the core bootstrap package. | . | .

fd3daaa7acd4.doc: Assessment of open standards for requirements and methodologies fitting the bootstrap Requirement
fd3daaa7acd4.title: 6. What this methodology refuses
fd3daaa7acd4.content: . | Refuses adopting ReqIF XML or OSLC RDF into bootstrap/. Bootstrap must remain free of external interchange baggage. | Refuses monolithic document SRS models (IEEE 830). Requirements in this platform are atomic, graph-addressable statements (req:<slug>#<key>). | Refuses requirements without success criteria. A requirement without an explicit verification method (test, inspection, review, analysis) and criterion is unauditable and refused by CI gates. | Refuses ad-hoc NFR categories. Non-functional categories must adhere to the established ISO/IEC 25010 quality model. | .

acc769bf693a.doc: Assessment of open standards for requirements and methodologies fitting the bootstrap Requirement
acc769bf693a.title: Assessment of open standards for requirements and methodologies fitting the bootstrap Requirement
acc769bf693a.content: ← All methodologies . requirements-standards-assessment — declared by cat-harness — source held . Applies when. Evaluating how requirements authored or verified in the harness map to or from open industry standards, interchange formats, statement grammars, and quality models — and deciding which transformations belong in higher harness layers (cat-harness, and content layers above it) while keeping the bootstrap Requirement schema strictly self-contained and free of external dependencies. It answers how bootstrap requirements translate to ReqIF, OSLC-RM, EARS, ISO 29148, and ISO 25010, what each standard costs in serialization and semantic complexity, and where mapping adapters must live. It does NOT govern runtime execution logs (prov-o-provenance), decision table structures (dmn), software package bills of materials (spdx-3), or access policy enforcement (odrl-policies). Origin. Survey and comparative assessment of formal and open requirements standards: OMG Requirements Interchange Format (ReqIF 1.2, formal/2013-10-01); OASIS Open Services for Lifecycle Collaboration Requirements Management (OSLC-RM 2.1 / OSLC Core 3.0); Easy Approach to Requirements Syntax (EARS: Mavin et al., IEEE RE 2009); ISO/IEC/IEEE 29148:2018 (Systems and software engineering — Life cycle processes — Requirements engineering); IEEE Std 830-1998 (Recommended Practice for Software Requirements Specifications, superseded by ISO/IEC/IEEE 29148); ISO/IEC 25010:2011/2023 (Systems and software engineering — Systems and software Quality Requirements and Evaluation — System and software quality models); INCOSE Guide for Writing Requirements (INCOSE-TP-2010-006-04, 4th Edition, 2023). Evaluated against the bootstrap Requirement schema (bootstrap/schemas/requirement.schema.json, Issue #1164). fca84a65de92.doc: Zero trust architecture (NIST SP 800-207) — trust is never granted implicitly, it is evaluated per request at a decision point
fca84a65de92.title: Zero trust architecture
fca84a65de92.content: Adopted on the owner’s ruling, 2026-10-07 (issue #2389, work item pk0z). The adversarial pass over the earlier draft (work item 1ygp, finding L3.1) showed that the draft was mostly this platform’s own rules presented as a method. The owner chose to split it, and asked to “make it a proper methodology” and to “ingest completely”. So this node holds only the method, as SP 800-207 states it. This platform applies it in the skill zero-trust-handover: the hand-over rules H1–H9, the hand-over screen and the sink-based risk table. That skill names this node and does not restate it, and this node does not restate the skill (methodology-adoption, §”Node, skill, or both?”).

1357c2083374.doc: Zero trust architecture (NIST SP 800-207) — trust is never granted implicitly, it is evaluated per request at a decision point
1357c2083374.title: What the method is
1357c2083374.content: The operative definition (sec-003-2-zero-trust-basics): . “Zero trust (ZT) provides a collection of concepts and ideas designed to minimize uncertainty in enforcing accurate, least privilege per-request access decisions in information systems and services in the face of a network viewed as compromised.” . The aim is stated as uncertainty to be reduced, not removed: “To lessen uncertainties (as they cannot be eliminated), the focus is on authentication, authorization, and shrinking implicit trust zones” (same section). The abstract model (Figure 1) puts one policy decision / enforcement point between an untrusted subject and a resource. The implicit trust zone behind that point is what the method shrinks.

5fd5de0b0242.doc: Zero trust architecture (NIST SP 800-207) — trust is never granted implicitly, it is evaluated per request at a decision point
5fd5de0b0242.title: The seven tenets (sec-004-21-tenets-of-zero-trust)
5fd5de0b0242.content: NIST calls these “the ideal goal”, and says “not all tenets may be fully implemented in their purest form for a given strategy.” . | “All data sources and computing services are considered resources.” | “All communication is secured regardless of network location.” — “Network location alone does not imply trust.” | “Access to individual enterprise resources is granted on a per-session basis.” — “authentication and authorization to one resource will not automatically grant access to a different resource.” | “Access to resources is determined by dynamic policy”, drawn from the observable state of identity, application and asset, and possibly from behavioural and environmental attributes. | “The enterprise monitors and measures the integrity and security posture of all owned and associated assets. No asset is inherently trusted.” | “All resource authentication and authorization are dynamic and strictly enforced before access is allowed”: a constant cycle of obtaining access, assessing threats, adapting and reevaluating trust. | “The enterprise collects as much information as possible about the current state of assets, network infrastructure and communications and uses it to improve its security posture.” | . The tenets’ own scope limit. They “apply to work done within an organization or in collaboration with one or more partner organizations and not to anonymous public or consumer-facing business processes. An organization cannot impose internal policies on external actors” (same section).

df300b875bef.doc: Zero trust architecture (NIST SP 800-207) — trust is never granted implicitly, it is evaluated per request at a decision point
df300b875bef.title: Six network assumptions (sec-005-22-a-zero-trust-view-of-a-network)
df300b875bef.content: . | The whole private network is “not considered an implicit trust zone”. Assets should “always act as if an attacker is present”. | Devices on the network may not be owned or configurable by the enterprise. | “No resource is inherently trusted.” Its posture is evaluated by a PEP, continually for the life of the session. | Not all enterprise resources are on enterprise-owned infrastructure. | Remote subjects and assets “cannot fully trust their local network connection”. | Assets and workflows moving between enterprise and nonenterprise infrastructure keep a consistent security policy and posture. | .

7435ea91e909.doc: Zero trust architecture (NIST SP 800-207) — trust is never granted implicitly, it is evaluated per request at a decision point
7435ea91e909.title: The logical components (sec-006-3-logical-components-of-zero-trust-architecture, Figure 2)
7435ea91e909.content: . | Policy engine (PE). “responsible for the ultimate decision to grant access to a resource for a given subject”. It takes enterprise policy and outside inputs into a trust algorithm, and “makes and logs the decision”. | Policy administrator (PA). Establishes or shuts down the communication path and issues session-specific credentials. It “relies on [the PE’s] decision”. The PE and PA together are the policy decision point (PDP). | Policy enforcement point (PEP). “responsible for enabling, monitoring, and eventually terminating connections between a subject and an enterprise resource.” It may be split into a client-side agent and a resource-side gateway, or be a single portal. | The inputs to the PE. Continuous diagnostics and mitigation, industry compliance, threat intelligence, network and system activity logs, data access policies, PKI, identity management and SIEM. | Two planes. The components talk on a control plane separate from the data plane that carries application data. | . Four deployed variations (sec-012 to sec-015; Figures 3–6) arrange the same components: . | device agent with a gateway; | an enclave behind one gateway; | a resource portal with no agent on the subject; | application sandboxes on a possibly compromised asset. | .

2fabd85f721c.doc: Zero trust architecture (NIST SP 800-207) — trust is never granted implicitly, it is evaluated per request at a decision point
2fabd85f721c.title: The trust algorithm (sec-016-33-trust-algorithm, sec-017-331-trust-algorithm-variations, Figure 7)
2fabd85f721c.content: The PE’s decision process. Its inputs are: . | the access request; | the subject database and its history; | the asset database and the asset’s observable status; | resource policy requirements; | threat intelligence and logs. | . NIST distinguishes algorithms on two axes: . | Criteria-based or score-based. A criteria-based algorithm grants access “only if all the criteria are met”. A score-based one computes a confidence level from “values for every data source and enterprise-configured weights” and compares it with a threshold. | Singular or contextual. A singular algorithm judges each request alone, with the “risk that an attack can go undetected if it stays within a subject’s allowed role”. A contextual one also weighs the subject’s recent history. | .

f544db4e7bbb.doc: Zero trust architecture (NIST SP 800-207) — trust is never granted implicitly, it is evaluated per request at a decision point
f544db4e7bbb.title: The threats NIST names for a ZTA itself (sec-026 to sec-033)
f544db4e7bbb.content: . | 5.1 subversion of the decision process: “any configuration changes must be logged and subject to audit”; | 5.2 denial of service or network disruption; | 5.3 stolen credentials and insider threat; | 5.4 visibility on the network; | 5.5 storage of system and network information; | 5.6 reliance on proprietary data formats or solutions; | 5.7 use of non-person entities (NPE) in ZTA administration. This is the one written about agents (sec-033-57-use-of-non-person-entities-npe-in-zta-adminis): . “Artificial intelligence and other software-based agents are being deployed to manage security issues … The associated risk is that an attacker will be able to induce or coerce an NPE to perform some task that the attacker is not privileged to perform. … If an attacker can interact with the agent, they could theoretically trick the agent into allowing the attacker greater access or into performing some task on behalf of the attacker.” . NIST calls how such agents authenticate “an open issue”. Its stated mitigation for their errors is “regular retuning analysis to correct mistaken decisions”. It names false positives and false negatives as “the biggest risk” of automated enforcement. | .

7031e5c1ad1f.doc: Zero trust architecture (NIST SP 800-207) — trust is never granted implicitly, it is evaluated per request at a decision point
7031e5c1ad1f.title: Migration (sec-042 to sec-052, Figure 12)
7031e5c1ad1f.content: A ZTA is introduced as a cycle laid against the NIST Risk Management Framework, not switched on: . | identify the actors; | identify the assets; | identify key processes and evaluate the risks of executing them; | formulate policies for a candidate; | identify candidate solutions; | deploy and monitor initially; | expand. | . “Incomplete knowledge will most often lead to a business process failure where the PE denies requests due to insufficient information” (sec-045-73-steps-to-introducing-zta-to-a-perimeter-based).

6f1b8f8d4f9e.doc: Zero trust architecture (NIST SP 800-207) — trust is never granted implicitly, it is evaluated per request at a decision point
6f1b8f8d4f9e.title: Where this rendering stops, and what is refused
6f1b8f8d4f9e.content: . | The enterprise network machinery is not adopted. That covers the CDM program, TIC 3.0, EINSTEIN, FICAM, micro-segmentation and software-defined perimeters (§3.1, §6). This platform is not an enterprise network. It adopts the decision structure (a named decision point, a named enforcement point, per-request policy, no implicit trust by location) and applies it to agents, tools and graphs. Deciding which components map to what is the skill’s business, not this node’s. | The score-based trust algorithm is refused. A score from “configured weights” reads as a measurement, and the weights are invented. That is methodology-adoption §”Never quantify a judgement to make it look measured”. Of NIST’s two kinds, only the criteria-based trust algorithm is adopted. | NIST’s applicability limit is kept as NIST states it. The tenets do not govern anonymous public participants, and an organisation cannot impose its policy on them. How this platform handles text from such participants is the skill’s business, not this node’s. | No performance or efficacy claim rests on this source. SP 800-207 is an architecture and guidance document. It reports no evaluation, and none is attributed to it here. | .

b5c589fd4152.doc: Zero trust architecture (NIST SP 800-207) — trust is never granted implicitly, it is evaluated per request at a decision point
b5c589fd4152.title: What the source does not establish
b5c589fd4152.content: . | How an agent should authenticate to the decision components. NIST leaves this “an open issue” (5.7), and so does this node. | Whether a pattern-based screen of agent input is adequate. NIST does not discuss prompt injection by name. The screen in the skill is this platform’s mitigation, judged against prior work held separately (CaMeL, DataFilter, DefensiveTokens), and is not an application of anything 800-207 says. | .

df62672d7e95.doc: Zero trust architecture (NIST SP 800-207) — trust is never granted implicitly, it is evaluated per request at a decision point
df62672d7e95.title: Zero trust architecture (NIST SP 800-207) — trust is never granted implicitly, it is evaluated per request at a decision point
df62672d7e95.content: ← All methodologies . zero-trust-architecture — declared by cat-harness — source held . Applies when. A participant is about to act on something another participant gave it, and the question is whether to trust it. That covers an access decision at a boundary, a hand-over between agents, a tool or a dependency graph reaching this platform, and the design of a check that decides any of these. It answers how trust is decided: never by location, per request, by policy, at a named decision and enforcement point. It is NOT a method for choosing among options (kepner-tregoe), for recording a decision (madr), for a recurring business rule (dmn), or for who is involved (raci). It is also not a threat-modelling or risk-scoring method: it says where trust is decided, not how likely an attack is. Origin. NIST Special Publication 800-207, Zero Trust Architecture, by Scott Rose, Oliver Borchert, Stu Mitchell and Sean Connelly, August 2020, doi:10.6028/NIST.SP.800-207. The primary is held, in full, at library/nist-sp-800-207: 59 pages, 55 sections and all 12 figures described. The owner supplied it on 2026-10-07 after this container’s network policy denied both NIST hosts. It is a US-government work: the PDF states it “is not subject to copyright in the United States” (p. i). Every quotation below is from that copy, cited by section id. 32b831e8614c.doc: Requirements filing and organisation — literature search, candidate methodologies, and filing process
32b831e8614c.title: Requirements filing and organisation — literature search, candidate methodologies, and filing process
32b831e8614c.content: This methodology node completes work item folio-assistant-qh1s (Issue #1164): a literature search over requirements-management practice across the five lifecycle dimensions (organisation, identifiers, traceability, change, and retirement), the explicit adoption or rejection of candidate methodologies through methodology-adoption, and the proposed executable BPMN filing process (sdlc/processes/requirements-filing.bpmn (opt-in cat-harness.sdlc)) put to the owner before automation is built. Whereas sibling methodology requirements-standards-assessment.md (work item folio-assistant-1gf7) assessed open interchange and syntax standards (ReqIF, OSLC RM, EARS, RFC 2119 / RFC 8174, IEEE 29148, Planguage, SysML, Gherkin) to map their constructs onto bootstrap/schemas/requirement.schema.json and bootstrap/schemas/requirement-set.schema.json, this node governs how requirements are organised, identified, traced, amended, superseded, and retired as they are filed into docs/requirements/ once docs/requirements/ grows past a flat hand-maintained list.

603ead93e9a8.doc: Requirements filing and organisation — literature search, candidate methodologies, and filing process
603ead93e9a8.title: 1. Literature search over requirements-management practice
603ead93e9a8.content: Per literature-search, every surveyed source is recorded below with its provenance/access status (ingested library/<bib-slug> node where held on disk, or external standard / open-source specification where copyright or scope keeps the full text outside library/) and with what it offers here across the five dimensions of work item folio-assistant-qh1s: . | Organisation — how a growing corpus of filed requirements is structured and navigated without breaking path stability. | Identifiers — how requirements and sub-clauses receive durable, collision-free, human- and machine-addressable IDs in a distributed Git workflow. | Traceability — how backward lineage (to proposals, user needs, and L1 sources), horizontal dependencies (between requirements), and forward verification (to work items, skills, processes, and test attestations) are recorded and checked. | Change — how in-scope amendments versus scope-altering replacements are distinguished, reviewed, and versioned. | Retirement — how obsolete or superseded requirements leave active force without breaking historical links or audit trails. | . 1.1 Summary matrix across the five filing dimensions . | Source | Provenance / library status | Organisation | Identifiers | Traceability | Change | Retirement | . | ISO/IEC/IEEE 29148:2018 (Systems and software engineering — Life cycle processes — Requirements engineering, Clauses 5.2.7, 6.4, 6.5) | Proprietary ISO/IEEE standard; assessed via public clause structure (no full-text redistributable PDF in library/) | Separates stakeholder requirements (StRS) from system/software requirements (SyRS/SRS); organises by system architecture or functional domain | Unique, persistent requirement identifier (id) independent of document section position | Clause 5.2.7 mandates bidirectional traceability: backward to source/parent need, forward to design elements and verification records | Clause 6.5 requires formal change control, impact analysis over dependent items, and baseline sign-off | Explicit lifecycle status attribute (retired / obsolete / superseded); historical records retained for audit | . | Volere Requirements Specification Template (Robertson & Robertson, Mastering the Requirements Process, 4th ed.) | Commercial book / template; assessed via published Volere atomic “Snow Card” specification | Groups requirements by functional area / business event / concern rather than implementation module; pairs functional with non-functional categories | Atomic requirement number + type code + event/use-case reference on each Snow Card | Each card records Source / Originator, Supporting Materials, Dependencies, and a mandatory measurable Fit Criterion | History log on the card tracking creation, amendments, and re-verification | Explicit archived / retired state with reason when business rules change; card number is never reused | . | IREB CPRE Foundation Level (Pohl & Rupp, Requirements Engineering Fundamentals, 3rd ed.) | Standard RE body of knowledge; external textbook | Contrasts tree-structured chapter hierarchies against faceted / attribute-driven views over atomic requirement objects | Recommends immutable object identifiers decoupled from chapter headings so restructuring views never renumbers requirements | Defines three explicit trace link directions: pre-RS / backward (to origins), post-RS / forward (to artefacts/tests), and within-RS / horizontal (dependsOn, refines, conflictsWith) | Configuration management and baseline versioning; change impact propagation along trace links | Status state machine (draft → agreed → validated → implemented → deprecated/retired) | . | Doorstop (Browning & Adams, Doorstop: Text-Based Requirements Management Using Version Control, JOSS 2014; github.com/doorstop-dev/doorstop) | Open-source Git-native requirements tool (lgpl-3.0); external software reference | Stores one text file per requirement (YAML or Markdown-with-front-matter) inside version-controlled directories representing document trees | Prefix + identifier per file, addressable in git diffs; supports sub-links and hierarchical parent pointers | Parent/child trace links stored directly in requirement front matter; detects suspect links when a parent requirement changes | Git commits and pull requests are the change-control log; review happens in PR diffs alongside code and tests | active: false / normative: false front-matter flags retire an item in place without git rm, keeping git blame and incoming links intact | . | Nygard ADRs & MADR 3.0.0 (Nygard 2011; Kopp et al., adr.github.io/madr/, already adopted in methodologies/madr.md) | Adopted harness methodology (methodologies/madr.md) | Flat directory of Markdown files (docs/decisions/ or docs/proposals/), indexed by concern or status in index.md | Filename slug (<slug>.md) serves as the stable human-readable identifier | Cross-references related decisions, issues, and motivating forces in front matter and body | Append-only / immutable intent: minor clarifications edit in place; substantive reversals file a new record that supersedes the old | Explicit status transitions: proposed → accepted → deprecated | superseded by ADR-XXXX; old files are never deleted | . | W3C PROV-O (PROV-O: The PROV Ontology, W3C Recommendation 2013, adopted in methodologies/prov-o-provenance.md) | Ingested in library/w3c-2013-prov-o | Graph of prov:Entity nodes linked by typed provenance relations independent of filesystem nesting | Stable IRIs (req:<slug>, req:<slug>#<key>) identifying each entity | prov:wasDerivedFrom (parent/source lineage), prov:wasGeneratedBy (filing/test activity), prov:wasAttributedTo (actor/sign-off) | prov:wasRevisionOf and prov:specializationOf distinguish revisions from distinct derived entities | prov:wasInvalidatedBy and prov:invalidatedAtTime model retirement/supersession without erasing the entity from the provenance graph | . | RFC 2119 & RFC 8174 (Bradner 1997; Leiba 2017 — BCP 14 key words) | Ingested in library/rfc2119-key-words-requirement-levels and library/rfc8174-uppercase-vs-lowercase-2119-key-words | Separates normative statements (MUST, SHOULD, MAY) from explanatory prose within a specification | Statement-level addressing (statements[].key → req:<slug>#<key>) so each normative keyword clause is individually citable | Pairs each uppercase keyword statement with its own successCriteria and verification witness | Changing a statement’s modality (SHOULD → MUST) is a normative change requiring re-sign-off | Retiring or relaxing a MUST statement requires explicit normative adjudication | . | Specification-Compiled Agents & Issue-Driven Work Plans (arxiv-2404.04834v4; hmans-2026-beans-readme) | Ingested in library/arxiv-2404.04834v4 and library/hmans-2026-beans-readme | Connects declarative specifications to executable agent work items (beans/) and automated verification gates | Cross-graph IDs: req:<slug> linked to work item IDs (folio-assistant-xxxx) and process IDs (Process_*) | Closed-loop compilation: requirement statement → work-plan work item → implementing skill/process → test attestation | Specification edits trigger deterministic re-check (check:requirements) across all linked sets and attestations | Completed work items archive when closed; filed requirements remain in-force as the persistent invariant until superseded or retired | . | IEEE Std 830-1998 (IEEE Recommended Practice for Software Requirements Specifications, superseded by ISO/IEC/IEEE 29148) | Historical IEEE standard (superseded); external baseline | Monolithic single-document SRS organised by deep numbered outline (3.1.1.1 Functional Requirement 1) | Positional section numbers (§3.2.4.1) tied to document outline location | External traceability matrices (spreadsheets) mapping section numbers to test cases | Document-level revision history table at the top of the monolithic SRS | Striking out or deleting sections in a new SRS edition, causing section renumbering unless placeholder sections are kept | . 1.2 Detailed source notes: what each source offers this harness . 1.2.1 ISO/IEC/IEEE 29148:2018 (Clauses 5.2.7, 6.4, and 6.5) . | What it offers here: . | Attribute canon (Clause 6.5): Defines the essential metadata attributes every managed requirement needs beyond its statement text: unique identifier, requirement status, source/origin, rationale, priority/modality, verification method/criteria, and trace links. Our bootstrap/schemas/requirement.schema.json directly embodies this attribute set (id, title, status, proposedIn, derivedFrom, dependsOn, statements[], beans, skills, processes, supersededBy). | Bidirectional traceability (Clause 5.2.7): Establishes that forward traceability alone (requirement → test) is half a system; backward traceability (requirement → originating proposal/need/source via proposedIn and derivedFrom) is what prevents gold-plating (orphan requirements with no stakeholder origin) and explains why a constraint exists when an agent later considers changing it. | Change and retirement discipline: Distinguishes an approved baseline from working drafts (RequirementSet.stage: draft → proposed → approved → accepted in bootstrap/schemas/requirement-set.schema.json) and requires any transition into or out of active force to carry human sign-off. | . | . 1.2.2 Volere Requirements Specification Template (Robertson & Robertson) . | What it offers here: . | Atomic “Snow Card” structure with Fit Criteria: Volere’s primary contribution is insisting that a requirement is not filed until its Fit Criterion (our statements[].successCriteria) is written beside the description (statements[].statement). A requirement whose fit criterion cannot be stated is still a proposal or open question. | Organisation by semantic concern / business domain: Rather than organising requirements by the code file they touch or chronological filing date, Volere organises requirements by functional domain / concern area so a reader auditing one domain sees all governing invariants together. In cat-harness, the eight canonical concern groups in code-lists/concern-group.json (sdlc, process, tools, kg, library, content, ui, conduct) already partition skills, processes, schemas, and tests; projecting filed requirements under those same eight concern groups in docs/requirements/index.md aligns requirement navigation with the rest of the knowledge graph. | . | . 1.2.3 IREB CPRE (Pohl & Rupp, Requirements Engineering Fundamentals) . | What it offers here: . | Decoupling identification and storage from presentation views: IREB highlights the classic failure mode of hierarchical specifications: when chapter structure is used as both the file path and the requirement ID, reorganising chapters breaks every incoming reference. Storing atomic requirements at stable paths with immutable IDs (docs/requirements/<slug>.md → req:<slug>) while providing faceted views (grouped by concern group, by RequirementSet, or by lifecycle status in docs/requirements/index.md) gives both stable URIs and structured human browsing. | Three-axis trace topology: Clarifies the distinction between backward trace (proposedIn, derivedFrom), horizontal trace (dependsOn between peer requirements), and forward trace (beans, skills, processes, and verification attestations). | . | . 1.2.4 Doorstop (Browning & Adams, JOSS 2014) . | What it offers here: . | Git-native file-per-requirement architecture: Doorstop proved that storing requirements as individual text files with YAML front matter and Markdown prose in the same Git repository as the implementation eliminates external ALM database drift. Every requirement filing, amendment, or retirement travels in the same pull request as the code, process diagram, and test attestation that implements or verifies it. | In-place retirement (status: retired / superseded): Doorstop retires requirements by flipping a front-matter status field rather than deleting the file (git rm), ensuring that historical commits, test runs, and child requirements never point to a missing file. | Suspect-link awareness: Doorstop flags downstream items when an upstream requirement changes. In our harness, check:requirements (scripts/check-requirements.ts) provides the deterministic equivalent: it verifies that every derivedFrom, dependsOn, and supersededBy target exists, that no cycle exists in derivedFrom, that no in-force requirement depends on a retired or superseded requirement without updating its own lineage, and that every RequirementSet at approved or accepted has a matching human requirement-signoff attestation and only in-force members. | . | . 1.2.5 Nygard ADRs & MADR 3.0.0 (methodologies/madr.md) . | What it offers here: . | Proposal-to-Requirement continuity (git mv + proposedIn): In cat-harness, a feature starts as a proposal in docs/proposals/<slug>.md (where options are weighed using Kepner-Tregoe, SWOT, and MADR). When the feature ships and is signed off, git mv docs/proposals/<slug>.md docs/requirements/<slug>.md promotes the file in place, preserving its slug, its git log --follow history, and the options analysis that justified it, while proposedIn records the commit SHA and path of the proposal before the move. | Immutable supersession chain: When a shipped requirement’s fundamental contract is replaced by a new design, the old requirement file is not overwritten into a different contract; instead, the new proposal is filed as docs/requirements/<new-slug>.md, and the old requirement’s front matter is updated to status: superseded with supersededBy: req:<new-slug>. | . | .

c31f0e72a5a4.doc: Requirements filing and organisation — literature search, candidate methodologies, and filing process
c31f0e72a5a4.title: 2. Candidate methodologies: adopted vs rejected with reasons
c31f0e72a5a4.content: Following skills/process/process-core/methodology-adoption.md, we do not invent an unattributed house method. We adopt four orthogonal practices from the surveyed literature—naming their origins, what is taken, what is left behind, and how each binds into bootstrap/schemas/requirement.schema.json and check:requirements—and we explicitly reject five candidate practices with documented reasons. 2.1 Adopted methodologies . M1 — Doorstop + MADR git-native file-per-requirement and two-level semantic identifiers (req:<slug> and req:<slug>#<key>) . | Origin: Doorstop (Browning & Adams 2014) for one-file-per-requirement in Git with YAML front matter + Markdown body; MADR (methodologies/madr.md) for human-readable <slug>.md filenames; RFC 2119 / RFC 8174 (methodologies/requirements-standards-assessment.md) for statement-level normative clauses. | What is adopted: . | Each filed requirement lives in its own Markdown file at docs/requirements/<slug>.md with id: req:<slug> matching its filename stem (^req:[a-z0-9][a-z0-9-]*$). | Individual normative clauses inside a requirement are declared in statements[] (key, modality, statement, successCriteria) and addressed as req:<slug>#<key> (^req:[a-z0-9][a-z0-9-]*#[a-z0-9][a-z0-9-]*$). | Across docs/proposals/ and docs/requirements/, every <slug> is globally unique: a slug exists either as an unshipped proposal in docs/proposals/<slug>.md or as a filed requirement in docs/requirements/<slug>.md, never both (check:requirements refuses a collision). | . | What is left behind and why: . | Doorstop’s auto-incremented numeric filenames (REQ001.yml, REQ002.yml) are left behind because concurrent feature branches in a multi-agent repository collide on sequential integers and opaque numbers hide meaning in prose and test logs. | Doorstop’s content-hash “fingerprint” clearing on whitespace edits is left behind because explicit lifecycle status + human requirement-signoff attestations (test/attestations/requirement-signoff/) provide stronger, semantically intentional governance than raw byte hashes. | . | . M2 — Faceted concern-group organisation (code-lists/concern-group.json) over flat docs/requirements/<slug>.md storage (Volere + IREB faceted view) . | Origin: Volere functional-area grouping (Robertson & Robertson) combined with IREB CPRE’s separation of stable storage identifiers from faceted navigation views (Pohl & Rupp), bound to the harness’s eight canonical concern groups in code-lists/concern-group.json. | What is adopted: . | Physical storage stays flat at docs/requirements/<slug>.md: Every filed requirement sits directly in docs/requirements/<slug>.md, preserving 1:1 path parity with docs/proposals/<slug>.md for git mv, keeping req:<slug> → docs/requirements/<slug>.md resolution O(1) without directory searches, and ensuring check:requirements (mdFilesIn) reads 100% of filed requirements. | Logical organisation in docs/requirements/index.md groups by two orthogonal views: . | By Concern Group (sdlc, process, tools, kg, library, content, ui, conduct from code-lists/concern-group.json), so a reader or agent working in a concern domain sees every in-force invariant governing that domain. | By Requirement Set (RequirementSet) and Lifecycle Status (in-force vs superseded / retired), so CRD baselines and historical records are cleanly separated from active invariants. | . | . | What is left behind and why: . | Physical subdirectory nesting (docs/requirements/<group>/<slug>.md) is rejected (see R3 below) so that reclassifying a requirement’s concern group or cross-cutting scope never breaks markdown links or requires a second git mv. | . | . M3 — ISO/IEC/IEEE 29148 + IREB + W3C PROV-O three-axis bidirectional traceability . | Origin: ISO/IEC/IEEE 29148:2018 Clause 5.2.7 (bidirectional traceability), IREB CPRE (backward / horizontal / forward trace links), and W3C PROV-O (library/w3c-2013-prov-o, methodologies/prov-o-provenance.md). | What is adopted: . | Backward traceability (to origin and parent sources): . | proposedIn: required on every requirement promoted from docs/proposals/<slug>.md (commit SHA + path: docs/proposals/<slug>.md), binding prov:wasDerivedFrom to the exact pre-move proposal revision. | derivedFrom: array of parent req:<slug> IDs or library/<bib-slug> L1 sources from which this requirement is derived (checked for existence and acyclicity by check:requirements). | . | Horizontal traceability (between peer requirements): . | dependsOn: array of req:<slug> IDs that this requirement relies on at runtime or design time (checked for existence by check:requirements). | . | Forward traceability (to work items, implementation, and verification): . | beans: work-plan work item IDs (folio-assistant-xxxx) that delivered or amended the requirement. | skills and processes: the Skill and Process (Process_*) nodes that implement the requirement. | Verification & Sign-off: test runs (test/runs/) and attestations (test/attestations/) citing req:<slug> or req:<slug>#<key>, plus RequirementSet membership and human sign-off attestations in test/attestations/requirement-signoff/<set-slug>.attestations.json. | . | . | . M4 — MADR / ISO 29148 immutable lifecycle for change, supersession, and retirement (proposed → in-force → superseded | retired) . | Origin: MADR 3.0.0 (methodologies/madr.md) and ISO/IEC/IEEE 29148 Clause 6.5 configuration & change control. | What is adopted: . | Four lifecycle states (status in requirement.schema.json): . | proposed: drafted in docs/requirements/<slug>.md (or in a RequirementSet at draft / proposed / approved stage) awaiting final delivery and acceptance sign-off. | in-force: shipped, verified, and accepted by human BA/owner sign-off; actively binds the codebase and knowledge graph. | superseded: replaced by a newer requirement; must carry supersededBy: req:<new-slug> (enforced by requirement.schema.json allOf rule and check:requirements). | retired: no longer applicable (the feature or constraint was intentionally removed without replacement); supersededBy is omitted, and the retirement rationale and authorising issue/bean are recorded in the document body. | . | Change decision rule (Amendment in place vs Supersession): . | In-scope amendment (edit in place, keep req:<slug>): When clarifying prose, adding a statements[] sub-clause, tightening a successCriteria check, or updating skills/processes/beans links without reversing the core invariant, edit docs/requirements/<slug>.md in place and record a fresh requirement-signoff attestation if its RequirementSet is approved or accepted. | Scope-reversing replacement (file req:<new-slug>, mark old superseded): When a new proposal reverses or fundamentally replaces an in-force requirement’s contract, file the new proposal at docs/requirements/<new-slug>.md (status: in-force, derivedFrom: [req:<old-slug>]), and update docs/requirements/<old-slug>.md to status: superseded with supersededBy: req:<new-slug>. | . | Set membership consistency: Because check:requirements enforces that an approved or accepted RequirementSet may only contain in-force (or proposed at approved stage) members, superseding or retiring a requirement requires updating any RequirementSet that lists it (replacing the old ID with req:<new-slug> or removing the retired ID under a re-signed set amendment). | . | . 2.2 Rejected candidate methodologies (with reasons) . | Candidate methodology | Verdict | Reason for rejection in this harness | . | R1 — IEEE Std 830-1998 monolithic SRS & positional section numbering (§3.2.1.4) | Rejected | Tying a requirement’s identifier to its outline position in a single monolithic file causes cascading renumbering whenever a section is inserted, split, or reordered. Renumbering breaks req: URIs in test runs, attestations, and work items, and a single monolithic SRS file creates constant Git merge conflicts across parallel agent branches. | . | R2 — Centralised sequential integer IDs (REQ-0001, FR-0042) | Rejected | In a distributed multi-agent Git workflow (worktrees, branches, subagents), two branches filing requirements concurrently will allocate the same next integer (REQ-0043) unless gated by an external lock server. Even when unique, opaque integers convey no domain meaning in test logs or prose compared to req:<slug>#<key>. (Note: FR-NNN may still appear as a local table label inside a single CRD proposal during discussion, but the canonical graph identifier is req:<slug>#<key>.) | . | R3 — Physical subdirectory sharding (docs/requirements/<group>/<slug>.md) | Rejected (kept as faceted index view in docs/requirements/index.md instead) | 1. check:requirements (scripts/check-requirements.ts, mdFilesIn) scans docs/requirements/ and docs/proposals/ non-recursively and enforces a 1:1 slug namespace between docs/proposals/<slug>.md and docs/requirements/<slug>.md.2. Many proposals span multiple concern groups (e.g., sdlc + process); forcing a single directory path would make paths brittle when concern boundaries evolve.3. Faceted grouping in docs/requirements/index.md delivers the navigational benefit of Volere/concern-group organisation with zero path churn. | . | R4 — ReqIF XML / OSLC RM RDF triples as the primary authored store | Rejected (consistent with requirements-standards-assessment.md) | XML UUID graphs and raw RDF triples are unreadable in GitHub PR reviews and cannot be naturally co-authored as prose + front matter by humans and agents. Our YAML front matter (bootstrap/schemas/requirement.schema.json) exports cleanly to JSON-LD (bootstrap/ns.jsonld) without burdening authors with XML. | . | R5 — Destructive deletion (git rm) of superseded or retired requirements | Rejected | Deleting docs/requirements/<slug>.md when a requirement is retired or superseded breaks historical provenance: past test/runs/, test/attestations/, beans/, and derivedFrom links would become dangling references. Keeping the file in docs/requirements/<slug>.md with status: superseded (supersededBy: req:<new-slug>) or status: retired preserves referential integrity across the graph. | .

4f6f2a94fd57.doc: Requirements filing and organisation — literature search, candidate methodologies, and filing process
4f6f2a94fd57.title: 3. Proposed filing process (sdlc/processes/requirements-filing.bpmn)
4f6f2a94fd57.content: To fulfil Criterion 3 of work item folio-assistant-qh1s (“a filing PROCESS proposed as BPMN, to be put to the owner before it is built”), the executable BPMN diagram sdlc/processes/requirements-filing.bpmn (Process_RequirementsFiling) models the end-to-end process for filing, organising,superseding, or retiring a requirement in docs/requirements/. 3.1 Where Process_RequirementsFiling sits in the lifecycle . In the CRDM lifecycle (skills/process/crdm/crdm-requirements-workflow.md): . | Phases 1–4 (crdm-needs.bpmn, crdm-requirements-definition.bpmn, crdm-data-model.bpmn, crdm-signoff.bpmn) produce and sign off a proposal in docs/proposals/<slug>.md (and optionally a RequirementSet moving from draft → proposed → approved). | Phase 5 (crdm-deliver.bpmn) builds and verifies the MVP in code, skills, and processes. | At Phase 6 (crdm-close.bpmn), when the feature ships and stakeholders/BA confirm acceptance criteria are met, Process_RequirementsFiling (sdlc/processes/requirements-filing.bpmn) governs the transition of the proposal into docs/requirements/<slug>.md (or the amendment, supersession, or retirement of an existing filed requirement). | . 3.2 Lanes and responsibilities . | Lane | Role (partitionElementRef) | Responsibility in Process_RequirementsFiling | . | BA / Feature Requestor (Lane_BA) | business-analyst | Reviews the filed requirement’s organisation, traceability links, normative statements, and any supersession/retirement transition (BA_ReviewFiling), and issues the human sign-off decision (approve, amend, reject, defer, cancel) required by check:requirements before a RequirementSet can reach accepted. | . | Authoring Agent (Lane_Agent) | authoring-agent | Executes the deterministic filing steps: classifies the requirement’s concern group and filing mode (A_ClassifyFiling), moves or updates the file in docs/requirements/<slug>.md (A_PromoteOrUpdate), binds the Requirement front matter (A_BindFrontMatter), updates superseded/retired records (A_UpdateLifecycle), indexes the requirement in docs/requirements/index.md (A_UpdateIndex), runs check:requirements (A_RunCheck), and records the human sign-off attestation (A_RecordFilingSignoff). | . 3.3 Step-by-step walkthrough of sdlc/processes/requirements-filing.bpmn . | A_ClassifyFiling — Classify filing mode, concern group, and req:<slug> identifier (skill: crdm-requirements-workflow): . | Determine which of the three filing modes applies: . | New filing from proposal: promoting docs/proposals/<slug>.md → docs/requirements/<slug>.md. | In-place amendment or supersession: amending an existing docs/requirements/<slug>.md or superseding req:<old-slug> with req:<new-slug>. | Retirement: retiring an obsolete docs/requirements/<slug>.md (status: retired). | . | Assign the primary concern group from code-lists/concern-group.json (sdlc, process, tools, kg, library, content, ui, conduct) for indexing in docs/requirements/index.md. | . | GW_FilingMode — Which filing transition? (cat-harness.processes:judgement): . | Branches on the three modes: promote (from docs/proposals/<slug>.md), amend-or-supersede (on an existing requirement), or retire (marking an active requirement retired). | . | A_PromoteOrUpdate — git mv proposal to docs/requirements/<slug>.md and capture proposedIn (skill: crdm-requirements-workflow): . | On the promote branch, record the pre-move commit SHA (git log -1 --format=%H -- docs/proposals/<slug>.md), execute git mv docs/proposals/<slug>.md docs/requirements/<slug>.md so Git history stays unbroken, and populate proposedIn: { commit, path: "docs/proposals/<slug>.md" }. | . | A_BindFrontMatter — Bind Requirement front matter, statements, and 3-axis lineage (skill: specification-management): . | Validate or author the YAML front matter against bootstrap/schemas/requirement.schema.json: . | id: req:<slug>, title, status: in-force (or proposed prior to acceptance sign-off); | statements[] with stable #<key>, RFC 2119 modality (MUST / SHOULD / MAY), normative statement, and measurable successCriteria; | Backward lineage (proposedIn, derivedFrom), horizontal dependencies (dependsOn), and forward implementation links (beans, skills, processes). | . | . | A_UpdateLifecycle — Update superseded or retired requirement records and RequirementSet membership (skill: specification-management): . | When superseding req:<old-slug> or retiring a requirement, set status: superseded + supersededBy: req:<new-slug> (or status: retired with retirement rationale in prose) on the old file without deleting it, and update any RequirementSet in docs/requirements/*.set.json so no approved/accepted set retains a non-in-force member. | . | A_UpdateIndex — Organise entry in docs/requirements/index.md under its concern group and status (skill: crdm-requirements-workflow): . | Add or update the requirement’s row in docs/requirements/index.md under its code-lists/concern-group.json section (for in-force requirements) or the Superseded and Retired Requirements archive table, and regenerate directory READMEs (subgraph-readmes.ts). | . | A_RunCheck — Run check:requirements gate (skill: specification-management): . | Execute bun run cat check:requirements to verify schema validity, slug uniqueness across docs/proposals/ and docs/requirements/, derivedFrom acyclicity, resolution of all derivedFrom / dependsOn / supersededBy / skills / processes references, and RequirementSet invariants. | . | GW_CheckPassed — Does check:requirements pass?: . | If fail, loop back to A_BindFrontMatter to fix schema, collision, or broken-link findings before asking a human reviewer. | If pass, proceed to BA_ReviewFiling. | . | BA_ReviewFiling — BA / Owner reviews filed requirement, organisation, and sign-off (calledElement: Process_Adjudication, skill: adjudication, fulfilment: person): . | The Business Analyst / Owner reviews the filed requirement, its concern-group placement in docs/requirements/index.md, its traceability links, and its verification evidence, deciding approve, amend, reject, defer, or cancel (adjudication-requirement-set). | . | A_RecordFilingSignoff — Record requirement-signoff attestation and set stage (skill: adjudication): . | Append the human decision to test/attestations/requirement-signoff/<set-slug>.attestations.json and update the RequirementSet stage (accepted on approval). | . | GW_FilingAccepted — Filing accepted?: . | approve / amend → End_RequirementFiled (“Requirement filed and indexed in docs/requirements/”). | reject / defer / cancel → End_FilingHeld (“Filing held or deferred — recorded with reason”). | . | . 3.4 Open design choices put to the owner before automation is built . Before any new CLI subcommand or schema extension is built on top of check:requirements, the following three design choices from this proposal are put to the owner: . | Concern-group tagging — index-only vs schema field: . | Option A (current zero-schema-change baseline): Keep bootstrap/schemas/requirement.schema.json unchanged (additionalProperties: false) and organise requirements by concern group in docs/requirements/index.md. | Option B (optional schema field): Add an optional "concernGroup" (or "concerns": string[] referencing code-lists/concern-group.json) to bootstrap/schemas/requirement.schema.json so docs/requirements/index.md can be generated deterministically from front matter. | . | Enforcing in-force dependency health in check:requirements: . | Today check:requirements verifies that every dependsOn and derivedFrom target exists. Should check:requirements also fail (or warn) when an in-force requirement dependsOn a requirement whose status is retired or superseded? | . | Standalone requirement sign-off vs RequirementSet sign-off: . | Today test/attestations/requirement-signoff/<set-slug>.attestations.json attaches to a RequirementSet (*.set.json), and a standalone docs/requirements/<slug>.md promoted via git mv only needs proposedIn. Should every filed requirement belong to a concern-group RequirementSet (docs/requirements/<group>.set.json), or remain standalone unless grouped by a CRD? | . | .
