a7aafb7490ee.title: Are the .jsonld siblings still in sync with their .ts manifests?
a7aafb7490ee.content: Process_JsonLdDrift · strict · 1 step(s) . Check that the committed .jsonld siblings are still in sync with the .ts manifests they are generated from. A GENERATED FILE THAT IS COMMITTED CAN GO STALE, AND A STALE ONE IS CONSULTED. Five --check runs in one job: the JSON-LD context, the block siblings, the library nodes, the site graph, and the label-resolution tests. Each regenerates from the .ts manifest that owns it and fails on any difference. They are drawn as ONE task rather than five, because they are independent of each other and sequential only because a single job runs them. Five boxes would assert an ordering the workflow does not have. The check itself is the shared generated-file-drift process (Process_GeneratedFileDrift), drawn once for every drift check. This diagram stays because its workflow’s job names Start_Change (# bpmn-node:), which is what lets check:workflow-coverage see the job. i

74c467f4f7f0.title: kg-navigation
74c467f4f7f0.content: The skill itself is skills/kg/kg-navigation/kg-navigation.md. This page is the package’s README, kept here because a skill package holds skills only. How an agent finds the knowledge graph, and the skill that governs its task, before it knows the layout. A skill package of the cat-harness knowledge graph, under skills/kg/. It is not a top-level layer, because a layer that declares no needs has no layer, and kg:detangle can then only report its edges as undetermined. It sits under the declared skills/ graph rather than in cat-harness/kg-navigation/skills/ because skill_fetch names a directly-held skills directory after its layer, which would serve this package as cat-harness. A subdirectory of skills/ takes its own basename as its package name, as folio-core and crdm do, so skill_fetch serves it as kg-navigation. It is not a declaration inside a declaration: skills/ owns this directory like every other package.

73b21f6f1fc4.title: If you are cold, read the skill, not the directory
73b21f6f1fc4.content: Ask for it: skill_list, then skill_fetch. Do not open a path under skills/ from memory. The graph a layer declares is what resolves, and a hardcoded path is how a skill goes missing the moment the layout moves.

3b592be1538b.title: Two bodies, one subject — do NOT delete one as a duplicate
3b592be1538b.content: | where | precondition | . | bootstrap/skills/bootstrap-kg-navigation.md | nothing installed — no MCP server, no skill_fetch, no beans, no build | . | kg-navigation.md | the tooling is reachable — the MCP pair, and the filesystem fallback | . They answer the same question under different preconditions, so neither is a copy of the other, and merging them would leave one caller unable to run what it was given. Bootstrap’s must stay in bootstrap: it is phase one with nothing installed, and a bootstrap that reached into another layer for its first skill would fail in the cold-start case it exists for. Keeping the two as separately named skills lets both be addressed without either shadowing the other. If you are about to “consolidate” these, first answer: which precondition does the surviving body assume? Whichever you pick, the other caller is broken. Do not put a count in either body. A count in prose is a claim nothing checks.

0a50458bca96.doc: Move the graph into its repositories
0a50458bca96.title: Steps
0a50458bca96.content: Every one of the 8 step(s) is documented. | step | lane | skill / sub-process | what it does | . | Create the repositoriesTask_Create | Administrator | kg-separation | The owner creates the content and tools repositories and their Pages. Fix a red rehearsal or a discovery miss where it is. Nothing is seeded from here; it goes back to the gateway, which re-asks. | . | Seed both repositoriesTask_Seed | Authoring agent | kg-separation | Seed main, then bring the content and the tools in as reviewed pull requests with their history, so neither repository’s first commit is unreviewable. The seed includes every publisher the declaration promises (sub-kg-lifecycle stage 10): a qa directory with storage needs .github/workflows/publish-qa.yml, the caller of the tools layer’s layer-qa-publish.yml, and test/results/ ignored. Without it the declared store is never written, and once the layer stops committing its results no reader finds them. | . | Re-point: livesAt, seam, mount or subscriptionTask_Repoint | Platform authoring agent | sub-kg-lifecycleupstream-version-adoption | In the new repository livesAt goes (absent means it sits at the root of repository) and platform.ts points at where the platform now is. The host consumes it as a remote mount (a source.remote instance in its root index.config.json) if it imports its code, or a subscription if it only reads its content, pinned to a commit while staging. Additive: the host keeps its copy. | . | Verify on a fresh cloneTask_FreshClone | Build pipeline | sub-kg-lifecycle | bun run cat sub-kg:verify-clone --repo <owner>/<name> --ref <branch> (Tool sub-kg-verify-clone): clone into an empty scratch directory with submodules and any sibling it needs, install, and run its own gates. Green, red or unknown, and unknown is never green. Nothing in a seed runs standalone until the seam is re-pointed, so a missing module shows here. | . | Parent consumes, additivelyTask_Consume | Platform authoring agent | upstream-version-adoption | The parent pins the pair (a commit while staging, a version once released) — a code dependency as a source.remote instance in its root index.config.json (remote-mount skill), never a submodule — repoints its imports, and keeps its own copy until it is green with the dependency declared. Where cat-harness.sdlc is switched on, this step is the opt-in process upstream-version-adoption (Process_UpstreamAdoption, sdlc/processes/upstream-version-adoption.bpmn); it is not called from here, because a layer without that sub-graph does not have it (owner card Q-OPTIN-CALLS A, 2026-11-12). | . | First releaseTask_Release | Publication manager | — | Tag each repository, publish /v<major>/. From here the two are versioned independently; a tools release lists the content majors it supports. | . | Every identifier dereferencesTask_Verify | Build pipeline | — | After the release is live, every published identifier resolves to the file it names. Where cat-harness.sdlc is switched on, this step is the opt-in process publish-verification (Process_PublishVerification, sdlc/processes/publish-verification.bpmn); it is not called from here, because a layer without that sub-graph does not have it (owner card Q-OPTIN-CALLS A, 2026-11-12). | .

75c6a780cbe0.doc: A knowledge graph leaves for its own repositories
75c6a780cbe0.title: A knowledge graph leaves for its own repositories
75c6a780cbe0.content: Process_KgSeparation · strict · 8 step(s) . Move part of a knowledge graph into repositories of its own: the content (files to read, no code) and its tools (the code that writes and checks it) separate as a pair, into two repositories, not one. kg-separation.md is the practice; this is its order and its gates. Stages 1-3 are graph-detanglement, reused rather than restated. EVERY GATEWAY IS A COMMAND. Tools closed? is check:tools-closure with the content’s no-code test and a byte-identity check on the generated files; Every identifier its file's path? is check:node-iris; Green alone? is the standalone rehearsal; Ready to seed? is seed:ready --layer <name> --rehearse, decided by decisions/seed-readiness-gate.dmn. A check that could not run stops the process rather than reading as clean. A PERSON DECIDES FOUR TIMES, AND THE ADMINISTRATOR LANE SAYS WHERE: whether to separate at all, whether to authorise the extraction, creating the repositories, and the cutover. Nothing is committed to the new repositories before they are created, and the parent keeps its own copy until it consumes the first release. VERSIONS: the pair starts at the content’s version at the split, then each is versioned on its own; a tools release lists the content majors it supports. Examples: bootstrap and bootstrap-tools; cat-harness and cat-harness-tools. DRAWN IN PHASES (owner, 2026-11-08): prepare, authorise, move and cut over are each their own diagram, called here; a loop that crosses phases is drawn at this level. i i i i i i i i

505720031b97.title: KG to public portal
505720031b97.content: Process_KgToPortal · advisory · 10 step(s) . How a knowledge graph reaches a public portal this repository does not run: select, serialize, package, sign, distribute, and verify on the portal’s side. Three decisions belong to the DEPLOYMENT and are drawn as gateways rather than as steps — the ingestion transport, the versioned store, and the signing scheme. A pipeline that picks one of those is asserting a decision nobody made. A CDN is a LAYER, not a publication host. PUBLICATION_HOSTS answers “what serves the rendering”; a cache answers “what stands between the server and the reader”, and the canonical URL stays the origin’s either way. i i i i i i i i i i

1c08114ea946.title: Lanes — who acts
1c08114ea946.content: | lane | role | what it does here | . | Editorial | editor | Two decisions, not one: E_Scope bounds what may leave the repository before the pipeline runs, and E_HumanEyes — reached only after S_Sign — approves what a reader will actually see, which merging to main does not. When GW_Budget rejects a package as over budget, narrowing scope here is the only way back in, so this lane is doing gatekeeping at both ends of the pipeline rather than once. | . | Deployment owner | publication-manager | Owns the numbers every other gate in the pipeline checks against: GW_Budget measures the package against D_Constraints’ figures, not a feeling. When GW_Transport has no default branch to take, this lane is the one that records the gap as still open — at D_Undetermined — rather than letting the build pick a transport nobody decided on. | . | Build pipeline | build-pipeline | Executes E_Scope’s decision as bytes — cut, serialize, package — precisely enough that GW_Budget can weigh the actual package rather than guess from the graph’s node count. Each step reports what it did rather than only succeeding, which is what lets an empty selection be told apart from one that never ran. | . | Attestation (GDHCN / WHO SMART Trust) | attestation-service | Signs after A_Package and before E_HumanEyes, so what a human approves downstream is exactly what got signed — reordering the two would let a reviewer approve bytes the signature no longer covers. Whether that signature covers the whole package, each asset, or both composed is a deployment choice this lane executes rather than makes. | . | Publish target | publish-target | The one lane whose action makes a URL live, which is exactly why a CDN in front of it is not drawn as a second lane — folding the cache in as a participant would make its URL look like the published one, and the canonical URL is this lane’s promise to keep, not the cache’s. Uploading and exposing stay two separate moments here rather than one, so a bad layout is still catchable before a reader can reach it. | . | Portal (external consumer) | external-registry | The only lane outside this layer’s control, so P_Verify checks against an external trust anchor — the GDHCN trustlist — rather than against anything the pipeline itself asserts. When that trustlist cannot be reached, this lane’s answer is unknown, and GW_Verified routes it the same way as a mismatch: to the last good version, never to a guessed pass. | .

98e9db5fd483.title: Steps
98e9db5fd483.content: Every one of the 10 step(s) is documented. | step | lane | skill / sub-process | what it does | . | State the constraints, with denominatorsD_Constraints | Deployment owner | kg-to-portal | Money, network traffic, graph size, latency. Each needs a NUMBER and each number needs a denominator, because a constraint with no denominator is a preference: “the graph is too big” is not a finding, “6.2 MB per publication against a 100 GB free tier” is. Say which figures were measured, which were quoted from a vendor, and which could not be obtained; a figure from a chat message is none of the three. | . | Decide what may leave the repositoryE_Scope | Editorial | kg-to-portal | EDITORIAL, and it is stage 1 rather than a filter bolted to the exporter. kg-export produces the WHOLE graph because inspection wants the whole graph; a portal wants what its readers may see. Running the second as the first is how a QA verdict, a bean’s blocking note or an unpublished draft reaches a public cache. Decided once, here, rather than at each consumer. | . | Cut the subgraph that leavesA_Select | Build pipeline | kg-to-portal | Apply the editorial scope mechanically and report what it removed. A selection that reports nothing cannot be told from one that ran over an empty rule. | . | Serialize to JSON-LDA_Serialize | Build pipeline | kg-export | kg-export, already built and host-agnostic by design. Every edge term declared {“@type”: “@id”} — without that coercion the document is a list of records that merely LOOKS linked, and the node IRIs are fragments of the document’s own @id so the graph is mergeable with anyone else’s. | . | Package with digestsA_Package | Build pipeline | kg-to-portal | The serialization alone is not a package. A package is an addressable set — the JSON-LD, the assets it references, and a manifest naming every file with its digest and byte count. The manifest is what makes a REMOVED file detectable, which a per-file signature cannot do on its own. | . | Sign the package and/or each assetS_Sign | Attestation (GDHCN / WHO SMART Trust) | kg-to-portal | THE TRUST ANCHOR IS GDHCN, SPECIFIED BY THE WHO SMART TRUST IG. READ OFF THAT IG rather than from general knowledge: a GDHCN trustlist distributes KEY MATERIAL as W3C DID documents, and says nothing about what you wrap your bytes in — the health-certificate envelope is a separate specification in the same IG, and a document package is not a health certificate. So what is settled is where a verifier GETS THE KEY, not what it verifies. A portal that can fetch the bytes but not reach the trustlist cannot verify, which is unknown and not a failure — air-gapped is a declared deployment value, so that case is answered rather than assumed away. Still OPEN and unread: the rotation and revocation model, and whether a document-package signature can be expressed for a GDHCN-aware verifier at all. Two schemes with different properties remain to choose between, and the trustlist does not choose between them. A PACKAGE signature over the manifest verifies the SET — nothing added, removed or altered — and must be reissued whenever any file changes. A PER-ASSET signature verifies one file independently, which is what an edge cache serving one asset can actually check, and it cannot detect a removal because there is nothing left to verify. They compose; composing them is the safer and more expensive default, and it is the deployment’s choice rather than the pipeline’s. | . | Human eyes on the rendered artefactE_HumanEyes | Editorial | continual-progress | Easy to drop because merging to main looks like an approval. It is not: merging approves the CHANGE, and this approves what a reader will actually see. A description cannot stand in for it (continual-progress). | . | Record the decision as still openD_Undetermined | Deployment owner | decision-audit | An undetermined decision is DATA, not silence. It is recorded with what it waits on and what would settle it, so the next session can tell “nobody has chosen” from “somebody chose and did not write it down” — the same third state bean-blocking keeps for a block with no expiry. | . | Publish to the origin (a cache may front it)A_Distribute | Publish target | kg-to-portal | Reach host behaviour through publication.host, never by assuming GitHub Pages’ behaviour — Pages CANNOT serve application/ld+json and a local server can. A CDN in front is a layer, not the host: the canonical URL stays the origin’s, and the cache is an accelerated route to the same bytes. Uploading and exposing are separable steps on purpose, because collapsing them removes the last moment at which a bad URL layout can still be caught. | . | Verify what arrived against what was signedP_Verify | Portal (external consumer) | kg-to-portal | Against a GDHCN DID trustlist, which means the verifier needs THE NETWORK and not only the bytes — the key is resolved from the trustlist rather than read out of the package. The trustlist is itself static JSON served from a CDN (tng-cdn.who.int), and its path is a hierarchical filter — domain, participant, key usage, with - as a wildcard — so a verifier fetches the slice it needs rather than the whole list. The stage that gets dropped, because every other stage produces something visible and this one produces nothing when it passes. A package that is signed and never verified is a package whose signature is decoration. A portal that CANNOT verify reports unknown — a portal nobody asked is not a portal that checked. | .

780939151782.title: Decisions
780939151782.content: Every one of the 3 decision(s) is documented. | decision | what decides it | branches | . | Within the stated budget?GW_Budget | Measured against D_Constraints’ numbers, not against a feeling. The gate is here rather than before packaging because the package’s own size is the quantity being judged, and estimating it from the graph’s node count is the guess this gate exists to replace. | within budget → Sign the package and/or each assetover budget → Refused — over budget | . | Which transport? (UNDETERMINED)GW_Transport | THIS GATEWAY HAS NO DEFAULT BRANCH: the ingestion method is not determined. Pull from the portal, push to an object store, a git fetch, a signed tarball on a schedule — they differ in cost, in who initiates, in what must be reachable from where, and in what happens when a publication is missed. The deployment answers using D_Constraints’ numbers; until it does, the diagram reaches here and stops. Drawing one branch as the obvious one would record a decision nobody made. | a transport was chosen → Publish to the origin (a cache may front it)still undetermined → Record the decision as still open | . | Verifies?GW_Verified | Answered by verifying what arrived against what was signed. signature and digests match serves the bytes; mismatch rejects them and keeps serving the previous version. | signature and digests match → Readers have the bytesmismatch → Rejected — serve the previous version | .

An L1 library’s catalogue is library/; a note about it is a folio; the page explaining how ingestion works is docs. | yes — just-the-docs renders it to a website | . | archimate | cat-harness/archimate (typologies/archimate.json) | ArchiMate models a layer holds, as Archi .archimate files (plain XML or Archi’s zipped archive), named by cat-archimate.config.json (cat-harness’s archimate subgraph). Every view, element and relationship in a model is a node of its own: a page and an IRI, keyed by Archi’s own id, and every view is drawn as SVG from the model’s diagram. | no | . | openapi | cat-harness/openapi (typologies/openapi.json) | OpenAPI 3 documents a layer holds, each verbatim beside a provenance node naming the repository, path and commit it was ingested from (cat-harness’s openapi subgraph). Every operation in a document is a node of its own: a page and an IRI under the layer’s docs. | no | . | fhir-artifact-index | fhir-harness (typologies/fhir-artifact-index.json) | The artefact index of a published FHIR Implementation Guide, reconstructed from its published output — every artefact by canonical URL and published representation, with the IG API’s JSON Schema / JSON-LD sidecars as an overlay where the IG publishes them. No IG publishes such an index itself, so every field records which file it came out of. | no | . | ig-annex | fhir-harness (typologies/ig-annex.json) | Annexes an IG’s narrative pages load on demand: an annexes.json (ig-annexes/v1) naming, for each annex, the page it belongs on, the file beside the declaration that holds it, and the columns its table shows before a row is opened. The IG site build (stage-ig-sites.ts, and ig-repo-site.ts compose for an IG repository’s own site) copies each file to assets/annex/ and mounts ig-annex.js on the page. A .md annex is appended to its page as written, so its links address that page (shownOnPublishedPages); check:ig-annex-links judges them from there. | no | . | ig-artifact-jsonld | fhir-harness (typologies/ig-artifact-jsonld.json) | One JSON-LD node per artefact of a FHIR Implementation Guide, written from its artefact index beside the artefact’s thin page (artifact/<Type>-<id>.jsonld): the FHIR RDF class, Dublin Core and schema.org identity, each representation as a schema:MediaObject, and PROV for a compiled copy. It is the asset a thin artefact page renders. Beside them, one index node (artifact/index.jsonld, folio-ig-artifact-index-jsonld/v1) lists every artefact in the Publisher’s order, each entry naming its node: what the thin artifacts and toc pages draw. | no | . | ig-ast | fhir-harness (typologies/ig-ast.json) | The IG Publisher’s abstract syntax tree of a FHIR Implementation Guide (its resources, their dependency edges and the build plan), ingested into the folio that uses the IG. One branch per IG package id; the IG’s own source need not be materialised. | no | . | ig-metadata-index | fhir-harness (typologies/ig-metadata-index.json) | The IG Publisher’s own metadata exports for one published IG, harvested verbatim — ValueSet→CodeSystem edges, CodeSystem uses, and extension/profile usage paths. Each export declares whether it was present, absent or never looked for, and a uses field that upstream declared and left empty is recorded as exactly that. | no | . | ig-pages | fhir-harness (typologies/ig-pages.json) | The pages of a FHIR Implementation Guide mirror, generated from its artefact index and the chrome of its template chain. Carried beside docs on the same directory: docs is how the site mounts them, and this kind is what says they are derived. | no | . | catalogue | folio-assistant-core (typologies/catalogue.json) | a remote catalogue modelled BY REFERENCE — communities, collections and items of a corpus the layer does not hold. Every node declares whether its bytes are here (materialized), elsewhere (referenced) or unestablished (unknown), and there is no default. Distinct from library: that is content which IS here, this is the shape of a collection of which almost none is. Shape in folio-assistant-core/schemas/catalogue.ts. | no | . | computation-witness | folio-assistant-core (typologies/computation-witness.json) | What a folio’s computations recorded: one <name>.witness.json per producer run, naming the engine, the script and its hash, the commit, and each assertion with its computed and expected values. Written by the producer and regenerated by re-running it; addressable from prose and wired to a content block through computation.witness. | no | . | dsa | folio-assistant-core (typologies/dsa.json) | Data sharing agreements (DSA building block B3): each version’s legal text at its immutable URL, a W3C DCAT 3 dcat:Resource and dcat:Distribution record carrying dcat:downloadURL and an SPDX SHA-256 spdx:checksum, and a W3C ODRL 2.2 Agreement citing that distribution via DCMI Terms dcterms:source. | no | . | glossary | folio-assistant-core (typologies/glossary.json) | Terms and what they mean, as W3C SKOS (folio-glossary/v1, schemas/glossary.ts): local terms, each authored, candidate or could-not-extract, linked to external SKOS concepts by exactMatch/closeMatch, and external concepts listed as members without being copied. A whole external scheme is a remoteGraphs entry with graphTypologies: ["glossary"]. The glossary kind is perInstance, so every folio built on this layer gets one. Rendered on the site’s glossary/ page with SKOS JSON-LD beside it; the swimlane ledger is one more source. Read with the glossary-terms skill; gated by check:glossary. | no | . | public-comments | folio-assistant-core (typologies/public-comments.json) | public comments on a document under review, and the change-sets that group them — one JSON each. Written by public-comment.ts; a comment is a todo subclass (public-comment/1.0.0 extends todo/1.0.0), a change-set is not. | no | . | references | folio-assistant-core (typologies/references.json) | A directory of this kind holds folio-reference/v1 nodes, one file per reference, named <key>.json. A node is a CSL-JSON item (id is the citation key) plus provenance (authored, catalogue, library or extracted), derivedFrom (the asset it was taken from) and heldAt (the library asset that holds a copy). It sits at references/<key>, where cat-harness resolveReferenceKey already sends every cited key, so a citation in the KG resolves instead of dangling. referenceToJsonLd reads it as Dublin Core and BIBO; toCslJson, toBibtex, toRis and toJsonLdGraph export any set of them. Shape in folio-assistant-core/schemas/reference.ts. | no | . | review-verdicts | folio-assistant-core (typologies/review-verdicts.json) | reviewers’ per-block verdicts — one folio-review-verdict/v1 JSON each, pinned to the block’s hash, committed on the feature branch. Not a todo: it asks for nothing. Read by the coverage gate (folio-review-coverage, bean px0t). | no | . | conjectures | folio-assistant-sci (typologies/conjectures.json) | A paper folio’s conjecture register — one folio-conjecture-register/v1 JSON node per open problem (schemas/conjecture-register.ts), pairing the source conjecture() block (conj:...) and its conjectureKind (formal vs identification) with its DMN-computed status (open, attempted, proved, disproved, superseded), Lean stub, critical-path theorems that assume it (assumedBy, computed as reverse edges over lean-formal-graph), and work-traceability attempts (attempts[]). | no | . | editor-checkers | folio-assistant-sci (typologies/editor-checkers.json) | A directory of this kind holds folio-editor-checker/v1 nodes. Each node names, for a content type and optionally a set of block kinds, the suggestion checker the ✍ suggest editor calls (checkSuggestion(before, after, ctx)) and the Crepe settings it applies: the latex feature config, node views, and remark plugins registered first. The editor lives in the shared edit-links runtime (cat-harness-tools src/core/edit-links.ts). It finds these nodes through the declaration rather than through a path anyone wrote down. | no | . | lake-cache | folio-assistant-sci (typologies/lake-cache.json) | Prebuilt Lake artefacts for a Lean package, one branch per package and toolchain on the Lean folio’s own repository, restored so a build starts warm. Declared by the folio that builds the Lean package; this harness owns the kind and the tool. | no | . | lean | folio-assistant-sci (typologies/lean.json) | Lean 4 sources. A directory of this kind holds Lake packages (each a lakefile.toml or lakefile.lean with its modules beneath it) or, in a harness, the Lean templates its tools instantiate. One graph per declared path: a folio with several packages declares each package directory, or their common parent. The nodes are modules (one .lean file each) and the declarations they elaborate to; a block’s lean.ref points at a declaration here. The visualiser is the package’s doc-gen4 render, built by the lean-html-docs tool and published under the folio’s site with the harness navbar and rail by lean-render-publish. | no | . | l1-extraction | smart-base (typologies/l1-extraction.json) | What the recommendation-extraction skill read out of ONE library entry, held beside it at library/<entry>/l1-extraction/ when the same instance holds the entry, or at l1-extractions/<entry>/ when the entry lives in another instance (smart-base’s handbook extraction, whose source moved to who-iris on 2026-10-30, who-iris#107): the L1 A-Box graph (l1.json, JSON-LD against the WHO SMART L1 ontology), the L2 scenario candidates derived from it (scenarios/scenario-candidates.l2.json), and the curation, vocabulary and run context that produced them. A sub-graph of library: nested in an entry, it is published with the entry beside the entry’s manifest; held apart, its own viewer (scripts/gen-l1-extraction-pages.ts) publishes it. It is never a folder named for an entry another library holds, which reads as a second copy of that entry and makes the library ingest refuse the duplicate slug. | no | . | web-annex | smart-base (typologies/web-annex.json) | A WHO publication’s web annexes, L1 or L2, held as data in the knowledge graph rather than as the files WHO attaches to the publication: a DAK’s core data dictionary workbook as JSON (dak-data-dictionary/v1, loaded on demand by the IG site’s annex view), and the declared mapping from its generic personas to the swimlanes of its business-process figures (dak-swimlanes/v1). cbce439d8139.title: The Knowledge Graph
cbce439d8139.content: TR… . On this page . | Two axes, and a word that already means a third thing | The subgraphs . | Schema | Content . | Scenarios | Workflows | Skills | Tools | Tests | Context | . | Harness | Dynamic Context | . | Which way the arrows flow | Repositories — four classes, three relations . | Content repositories | Tool repositories | Test repositories | Consumer applications | Three relations run between repositories | . | What is declared today, measured | Where the rules live | . This page is generated from docs/source/concepts-knowledge-graph/ — each section below links to its own source. ✎ Edit QA… TR… . Everything this harness knows about itself is one graph: the Schemas that describe its content, the Skills an agent reads, the Workflows those Skills are invoked from, the Roles that own a lane, the Tools and Tests that exercise a Skill, and the running record of what is being worked on. That graph is the Knowledge Graph, bootstrap’s own term for it. Two sentences fix the whole model, and the rest of this page elaborates them. An Agent utilizes Skills to execute one or more Tasks in a Workflow, with an associated Knowledge Graph of Static Context (Skills, User Stories) and Dynamic Context. Zero or more Tools may be associated with a Skill, for Test execution on an agentic-to-deterministic spectrum. Knowledge Graphs are managed in git repositories, comprised of self-documenting JSON-LD. Content is rendered into various formats for consumption by downstream knowledge products, and by public-health, clinical-health and personal-health applications. Three definitions come straight out of the first sentence and are used unchanged throughout: . | A Role is a swimlane, played by a human, agentic or mechanical Actor. | A Task is a step in a Workflow — a node in the BPMN. | A Skill is a Capability with defined inputs and outputs. | . The Knowledge Graph is not one directory, and not one repository. A layer declares the directories it scans and the kind of graph each holds, in its <name>.json root declaration; a dependent layer inherits those and may add its own. So the Knowledge Graph of a checkout is the union of what every layer in it declares — which is why “where is the Knowledge Graph” has no filesystem answer, and why a consumer asks for a kind rather than opening a path. This page says what the subgraphs are, which way the references between them run, how repositories divide the work, and how much of it is declared today. It does not restate the declaration mechanism: that is directory-conventions, and the schema is schemas/cat-harness.ts.

e07fb4d6c2b8.title: Two axes, and a word that already means a third thing
e07fb4d6c2b8.content: ✎ Edit QA… TR… . Two independent questions get asked about every subgraph, and neither answer implies the other. What is it about? Schemas, Skills, Workflows, Roles, Tools, Tests, Context, running state. This is the topical axis, and it is what the next section describes. Does it change while a Workflow runs? This is the Static Context / Dynamic Context split from the anchor sentence above, and the declaration already answers it mechanically in the holds field of each kind: a graph is content (a process produces it), context (a process reads it and never writes it), state (a process writes it as it runs), or derived (something else computes it). |   | holds | examples | . | Static Context | content, context, derived | Skills, User Stories, Schemas, Workflows, methodologies, memories | . | Dynamic Context | state | work items, todos, Workflow instances, QA sidecars | . A step that writes to a context graph is a defect rather than an update, which is the whole reason the field is REQUIRED — a kind that has not decided does not compile. The two axes are orthogonal. Skills and Schemas are both Static and are nothing like each other topically; memories and methodologies are both Static for entirely different reasons. Asking “is this a Skill?” tells you nothing about whether a Workflow may write to it, and asking “may a Workflow write to it?” tells you nothing about what it is for. Subgraph has a second meaning. Subgraph viewers uses it for one declared directory — the thing a visualiser draws and a Skill governs. This page uses it for a branch of the topical taxonomy. One topical subgraph is usually several declared directories across several layers, so the two readings are related but do not count the same things. Where the number matters, this page says declared directory or graph typology and leaves subgraph for the taxonomy.

d66d98768af1.title: The subgraphs
d66d98768af1.content: ✎ Edit QA… TR… . Schema . Every managed node has a definition — Zod authoritative, JSON Schema and JSON-LD generated from it — saying what shape it takes and what its fields mean. The Schema subgraph holds those definitions. It arrives empty except for what is self-describing. A bare harness knows how to describe a declaration, a directory and a kind; everything else is contributed by the layer that introduces it. A harness that adds a content kind adds its Schema in the same change, or the kind is unvalidated and its documents are told apart by shape — which is the failure directory-conventions names when it says the files declare what they are. Used for: validation at read time, the generated schema reference, and the @context a published Knowledge Graph is parsed against. Content . Instances of knowledge assets — the authored material a Schema describes and a Skill governs. Catalogues, documentation pages, themes, boards, translation sources, artefact indexes. Four subgraphs below are kinds of Content, listed separately because they are referenced differently, not because they are something else. Used for: everything a reader or a renderer consumes. Scenarios . Actors, the Roles they can take, and the User Stories those Roles are there to serve. An Actor is a concrete participant — person, agentic or mechanical — and persists across Workflows. A Role is the swimlane: a persona an Actor takes on because of the lane it is acting in, carrying the Skills that lane needs. Nothing is a reviewer; somebody acts as reviewer for the duration of a lane, and the same Actor is a different Role in the next diagram. Used for: binding a lane to what its occupant is expected to know, and auditing whether a Role’s Skills actually cover its lanes. Workflows . Business process as BPMN, with DMN for the decisions. Prefer Workflow over process throughout, because using both interchangeably costs more than the synonym buys. The diagrams are executable rather than illustrative. A lane binds a Role, an activity names the Skill to run, and a gateway MAY compute its branch from a DMN table. Instance state is committed, so a sibling session reads the same position rather than inferring one. Used for: running the work, and being the single answer to “where are we”. Skills . A Capability with defined inputs and outputs — the instruction body an Actor needs to perform a Task, stated generically so that it is portable across forges, binaries and machines by construction. A Content repository MUST constrain those inputs and outputs with a Schema; why is in Repositories below. A Skill MAY be designated mechanical, human, or either. That is a property of the Capability, not of whoever happens to run it today. Tools . The concrete mechanisms. A Tool names the Skills it satisfies through its satisfies field, and one Skill MAY be satisfied by several Tools. Used for: keeping the mechanism out of the instruction. A Skill that names a vendor, a CLI or an endpoint has swallowed a Tool, and the swallowing is what makes a layer un-portable. Tests . What adjudicates whether a Skill was performed, and how well. A Test exercises a Skill; the Tools associated with that Skill are what a Test runs it through. So the chain reads Test → Skill → Task, and a Test that names a Tool directly has jumped the Skill and measures a mechanism rather than a Capability. Used for: quality control, compliance testing, and comparing model performance across modalities. Tests are the third repository class below. Context . README files, memories, methodologies, recorded confirmations: what changes the conditions a Workflow executes in, without changing during execution. Applying a set of it deliberately — a Context Overlay — is what lets the same Workflow be run twice and the difference attributed to the context rather than to chance. Used for: repeatable testing across conditions. Covered in full by Managing agent context. Harness . The layer that renders the rest: the JSON-LD export, the visualisers, and the documentation. Its obligation is stated as four separate requirements because they fail differently — nothing serves it, nothing draws it, nothing says what it is for, nothing an agent can invoke against it. Used for: making a declared directory something a person can actually look at. A directory nobody can see is one nobody checks. Dynamic Context . What is being worked on and how far it got. Written by processes as they run, committed so it survives a fresh container. It splits by who the state is for, which is a sharper line than what the state holds: . | work items — agentic state management. Used by Agents to coordinate and track internal state within a Workflow. “Changes to the vaccination schedule are ready for review at staging.” | todos — human state management. Attached to a step in a Workflow or to a knowledge asset, for human Actors. “Please review this change in medication.” | . A todo attaching to a knowledge asset and not only to a step is what makes the two stores genuinely different rather than one store with an audience field: a work item without a Workflow position is incomplete, and a todo on a chapter has no Workflow position to be missing. Workflow instances, QA sidecars and health results are Dynamic Context too, written by the process that produces them. Used for: the work plan, and the evidence that a claim about the corpus was measured rather than remembered.

ed0f46e51567.title: Which way the arrows flow
ed0f46e51567.content: ✎ Edit QA… TR… . A reference has a direction, and the direction is what makes the graph answerable. Every edge below is carried by a named field in a schema, so it can be followed mechanically rather than inferred: . | from | field | to | . | Actor | roles | Role | . | Role | skills | Skill | . | Voice | activeIn.roles | Role | . | User Story | role | Role | . | Workflow activity | <bootstrap.processes:skill ref> | Skill | . | Workflow lane | partitionElementRef → <bpmn:resource> | Role | . | Workflow activity | <cat-harness.processes:bean op> | a work-plan operation | . | Tool | satisfies | Skill | . | Skill, Capability | satisfies | Requirement statement | . | Skill | graph-typologies | Graph typology | . | Skill | input, output | Schema (its contract) | . | Test run | skill | Skill | . | any content node | $schema | Schema | . | Folio | the board layer | Board, then Position, then Note | . Three properties of that table: . Skill is a sink. Roles point at Skills, Workflow activities point at Skills, Tools point at Skills, Tests point at Skills — and a Skill points at none of them. It names a Capability and does not know who holds it, what runs it, or what measures it. That is what lets one Skill serve several Roles, be satisfied by several Tools and be exercised by several Tests without editing the Skill. It is also why the chain reads Test → Skill → Task rather than Test → Tool. A Test that names a Tool directly has jumped the sink and is measuring a mechanism instead of a Capability — which is exactly the comparison the several Tools per Skill allowance exists to make possible. The Harness points at everything and nothing points back. A board is a diagram of a folio in the OMG sense that a BPMNDiagram is a diagram of a bpmn:process: the folio carries what is true, the layout layer carries where it was drawn, and the arrow runs folio → board → position → note and never back. A folio is complete with no board. The same asymmetry holds for every visualiser: removing the rendering layer loses the picture and no content. Workflows reference Context and never write it. The holds field makes that enforceable rather than conventional — a step writing into a context graph is a defect, not an update. This is the edge that makes a Context Overlay possible at all: if a run could mutate its own conditions, replaying it under the same conditions would not be a thing you could ask for. User Story works this way too. CRDM produces Workflows, User Stories and Roles, and Scenarios is where the User Stories belong. Each story is a node in scenarios/stories.json that names its role, so it can be pointed at, counted and traced to a Workflow, and the role names none — the same direction as a voice, which points at the role it addresses.

5a963235cf19.title: Repositories — four classes, three relations
5a963235cf19.content: ✎ Edit QA… TR… . A Knowledge Graph is managed in git repositories, comprised of self-documenting JSON-LD, and rendered into whatever formats a downstream knowledge product, public-health system, clinical system or personal-health application needs. That makes a repository the unit of distribution, and repositories come in four classes. A class is defined by what it is ALLOWED to do, not by what it happens to contain. Content repositories . Where the Knowledge Graph itself lives. A Content repository: . | MAY define Schemas for the Content types of a Knowledge Graph’s nodes. | MAY instantiate instances of those Content types. | MAY define the Skills needed to publish and consume those instances. | MAY designate a Skill as mechanical, as human, or as either. | MUST constrain a Skill’s inputs and outputs with Schemas. | . That last clause is the only absolute requirement in the model. A Skill is a Capability with defined inputs and outputs; a Tool claims to satisfy a Skill; a Test claims to exercise one. If the Skill’s boundary is not written down as a Schema, “does this Tool satisfy that Skill?” has no answer anyone can check, and the agentic-to-deterministic comparison the Tool and Test classes exist for cannot be run at all. Tool repositories . Where the mechanisms live, out of the Content repository on purpose. A Tool repository: . | MAY implement a Skill through coordinated use of Tools — scripts, retrieving and running software, remote or local services, containers. | MAY expose Tools to agents as MCP services. | MAY expose a Tool for local execution. | MAY configure Tools for a test harness. | MAY define more than one Tool for one Skill. | . The last one is the point of the separation rather than an allowance. Several Tools for one Skill is what lets the same Capability be exercised at different points on the spectrum from fully deterministic to fully agentic, and compared. Test repositories . Where adjudication, quality control and compliance testing live. A Test repository: . | MAY contain test data. | MAY contain test-data generation templates and configuration data. | MAY define Test Plans. | MAY define test-language dialects such as Gherkin. | MAY make test data available to a test harness, or to a subject-matter expert or author for review. | . Consumer applications . The downstream end. A consumer application: . | MAY use a Knowledge Graph’s Schemas and instance data from a Content repository. | MAY execute decision logic or indicator calculation from a Content repository. | MAY use Test and Tool repositories when building, preparing for a connectathon, or compliance-testing. | . Three relations run between repositories . Each edge has its own carrier in the declaration: . | relation | runs | carried by | . | depends | Content → Content | needs in the declaration — the layer stack, foundation first | . | references | Tool → Content, Test → Content | remoteGraphs — a graph this layer knows about and does not hold | . | utilizes | Tool → Tool, Test → Tool, App → Content, App → Test | dependencies in the config — what this layer USES, overlaid | . | associated | any harness ↔ any harness | associatedHarnesses — a harness this one knows, and where it is published; never loaded or materialized (skill associate-harness) | . Associated is a fourth, and it fixes no order: it is how a folio in another repository, such as ihris, is listed without being built here. The three answer different questions, so collapsing them loses information a consumer needs. Depends is about layering: it fixes an order, so a cycle in it is a defect. References is about knowing a graph exists without holding it, so it crosses a repository boundary by definition. Utilizes is about consumption at run time, and a consumer application may utilize a Content repository it has no dependency on whatsoever.

8c53b56bf069.title: What is declared today, measured
8c53b56bf069.content: ✎ Edit QA… TR… . The taxonomy above is what the Knowledge Graph is for. What the registry can actually produce is narrower: the taxonomy is not an inventory. Re-derive rather than quote: bun run cat kg:export dumps the graph, and instanceRootsIn plus readDeclaration give the directory census directly. Each registered kind is in one layer of holds — content, state, context or derived. Two kinds are renderable: docs and folio. Renderability is what wires a graph to the site build; every other graph reaches a reader through a visualiser the Harness layer builds over it, never by being published directly. Skills, Workflows and Scenarios are separate kinds — skills, processes and scenarios — so “give me the Workflows” is a query on kind, not a match on a path. cat-harness is still a kind and is not deprecated. An alias cannot express a split: GRAPH_TYPOLOGY_ALIASES maps one name to one name. On an entry declaring ["schemas", "cat-harness"] it means a schema IS a knowledge-graph node, which is why the skill scanner tests for the kind exactly rather than for its presence. It now means harness knowledge-graph content whose directory holds more than one part of it. A downstream declaration still saying ["cat-harness"] keeps parsing and keeps being scanned for Skills; it does not get the finer query. A directory inside another declared directory is not reached by convention. It declares its own kind, or a consumer filtering on kind never finds it. The generated process index reports such a directory as an orphan rather than quietly indexing fewer diagrams. One mismatch between the axes: fsh-guts is registered context, though it is topically Dynamic State. It is read by processes and not written by them, which is what context asserts. How a dependent contributes into a shared body of knowledge. Through the kind, and that is the mechanism rather than a stopgap. Each layer that contributes a Voice declares its own voices/ directory of kind voices, and the overlay resolves them together. A new contributor declares a directory, names the kind, and is done: no nesting, no subgraph declaration, nothing added to the schema. Nested subgraph directories are not used because they buy a hierarchy nothing needs, at the cost of a schema change and a migration of every declaration, while the overlay already delivers the outcome.

02f39634c8d7.title: Where the rules live
02f39634c8d7.content: ✎ Edit QA… TR… . This page is a map. The discipline is in the Skills, and where a Skill and this page disagree, the Skill wins and this page is wrong. | question | where it is answered | . | How a layer declares its directories, and every graph typology | directory-conventions | . | What content, context, state and derived each promise a consumer | content-context-and-state-graphs | . | Actors, Roles, Permissions, and why a Role is a swimlane | role-model | . | Authoring a Workflow activity, and what a bean-marked step performs | bpmn-processes | . | Which store answers which question about a running Workflow | workflow-state | . | Why a Skill states a capability and a Tool the mechanism | skills-and-tools | . | Context Overlays, and the several ways context is generated | Managing agent context | . | What a visualiser owes a declared directory | Subgraph viewers | . The schema behind every declaration on this page is schemas/cat-harness.ts; the Role and Actor shapes are in scenarios/roles.json and scenarios/actors/; the Tool shape is schemas/tool.ts. The audit that checks these joins actually resolve is bun run cat kg:audit, one criterion per join, written as committed QA sidecars so that “unbound since it was drawn” and “broken in the commit under review” stay distinguishable.

b713fc9fc9f3.doc: L1 document ingestion — a document to the L1 source knowledge graph
b713fc9fc9f3.title: L1 document ingestion — a document to the L1 source knowledge graph
b713fc9fc9f3.content: Process_L1DocumentIngestion · advisory · 16 step(s) . L1 document ingestion — a document to the L1 source knowledge graph. The harness holds only the basic, high-level document-ingestion flow; the detailed ingestion and cataloguing method is here. IT REFINES THE HARNESS FLOW BY CALLING IT. CallActivity_Basic runs the harness’s Process_Ingestion first — accept the upload, put its metadata into the KG, catalogue the asset in library/ — and this process then reads the document into a complete L1 entry. That is the inversion the harness skill library-ingestion describes: the call points DOWN, from core to the harness, and nothing in the harness names this process. edf34805628c.doc: L1 document ingestion — a document to the L1 source knowledge graph
edf34805628c.title: Steps
edf34805628c.content: Every one of the 16 step(s) is documented. | step | lane | skill / sub-process | what it does | . | Basic ingestion (harness)CallActivity_Basic | Ingestion Engine (agent, runs unattended) | calls Basic ingestion — an upload to an asset catalogued in library/library-ingestion | The harness’s document-ingestion.bpmn: accept the upload by a declared route, extract its metadata into the KG, and catalogue the asset in library/ — placed if materialized, recorded as referenced if not. Everything below refines that result for a document. Called, not copied. | . | Detect media type, mint a doc idTask_Detect | Ingestion Engine (agent, runs unattended) | document-intake | Sniff the media type rather than trusting the extension, and mint the doc id from the page-1 arXiv stamp where there is one, else from the filename. | . | Establish the licence from the uploadTask_Licence | Ingestion Engine (agent, runs unattended) | document-intake | EARLY: before any derivation, because library/ is holds: content and anything derived first is committed, so refusing it later is a deletion nobody may take unasked. This step sees only the upload itself — the licence recorded in its intake.json (the same stated / unknown record a library manifest carries) and whether a LICENSE file sits beside it. It never infers a licence from extracted text. The verdict is stated, unknown, or UNDETERMINED, and undetermined is never reported as cleared: the pipeline proceeds and says so, because a licence that only extraction can reveal is a later check’s to find. | . | Extract structureCallActivity_Extract | Ingestion Engine (agent, runs unattended) | calls Ingestion subprocess — extract structuredocument-intake | See ingest-extract-structure.bpmn. | . | Derive content from the assetsCallActivity_Derive | Ingestion Engine (agent, runs unattended) | calls Ingestion subprocess — derive content from the assetsdocument-intake | See ingest-derive-content.bpmn. Most of this subprocess is not implemented yet. | . | Ingest the themeCallActivity_IngestTheme | Ingestion Engine (agent, runs unattended) | calls Ingestion subprocess — ingest a themetheme-art-intake | See ingest-theme.bpmn. The subprocess derives one Theme node with kind sticky|webpage|publication, and refuses a source it cannot complete rather than emitting a partial theme. | . | Open the beanCall_BeanOpen | Ingestion Engine (agent, runs unattended) | calls Open the beanbean-coordination | Process_BeanOpen: check before you create, find out whose the bean is, and claim it — or leave it alone when it is someone else’s. The one place a claim is drawn; the gateway after this reads which end it reached. | . | Close the beanCall_BeanClose | Ingestion Engine (agent, runs unattended) | calls Close the beantodo-manager | Process_BeanClose: end the bean in a state that says why — complete and archive it, scrap it with its reasons and archive it, or record the blocker and hand it back. The one place resolve and archive are drawn; placed straight before the end so the engine’s resolve sees nothing left but the archive step. | . | Build the L1 knowledge graphCallActivity_BuildKg | Ingestion Engine (agent, runs unattended) | calls Ingestion subprocess — build the L1 knowledge graphdocument-intake | See ingest-build-l1-kg.bpmn. | . | L1 completeness gateCallActivity_Gate | Ingestion Engine (agent, runs unattended) | calls Ingestion subprocess — the L1 completeness gatel1-document-ingestion | See ingest-l1-completeness-gate.bpmn.Skill-backed by l1-document-ingestion: its section“What a complete L1 entry holds” names check:l1-complete as the gate andstates its three results.The gate contains one adjudication (Task_FlagDrift: real, spurious or source-wrong), and its own Task_Verdict records the answer as a reason against the verdict before returning. So both answers reach this step, and nothing here branches on them; Gateway_Complete branches on the gate’s completeness verdict instead. | . | Record the gap as a beanTask_OpenBean | Ingestion Engine (agent, runs unattended) | todo-manager | A missing derived artefact is a tracked gap, not a silent omission. The document stays in uploads/ until the gap closes. | . | **Move into library//**`Task_Promote` | Ingestion Engine (agent, runs unattended) | document-intake | The folder name IS the bibliography citation key, so a citation and a directory are the same string. | . | Publish the extracted statementsCallActivity_PublishStatements | Ingestion Engine (agent, runs unattended) | calls Publish extracted statements with source linkspublish-extracted-statements | THE ENTRY IS COMPLETE HERE, so its statements are published here. Every statement the extraction captured from this entry (a recommendation, a requirement, a candidate a person still has to rule on) becomes readable in two places: the folio’s working artifact, in the pages its content profile renders, and the shared extraction viewer. Each one links back to the library entry and to the section it came from.WHY IN INGESTION AND NOT LATER. A statement nobody can read beside its source is reviewed from memory, or not at all. Publishing when the entry is promoted means a reviewer can check every extracted statement against its source the moment it exists.The sub-process is the same for every content type. The content type decides only how its pages look, through its adapter. An entry that yields no statements (a referenced source, a dataset) passes through it with nothing to publish, and says so. | . | Summarise prose blocks, in every languageTask_SummaryQueue | Ingestion Engine (agent, runs unattended) | l1-document-ingestion | A QA sidecar of general document ingestion, drained slowly.Nothing is written to ENQUEUE a block: the queue is derived (every prose block in every declared library, minus those whose summaries.json record is a current draft or confirmation), so a promoted entry is in it the moment its blocks are. A re-ingested document whose text changed re-enters it on its own, because the record’s source_hash no longer matches.What an agent doing ingestion work does here is DRAIN a few: bun run cat summaries:next -- --n K hands it the next K blocks with their text, it writes a short summary of each in its own words, and bun run cat summaries:record writes them into library/<bib-slug>/summaries.json as drafts naming the agent and its model. The block itself stays verbatim and ingested.A library can ask for a summary in more than one language (who-iris: the six UN languages, owner 2026-11-11): the English draft, one in the document’s own language read from the source, and translations of the English into the rest, each its own narrative in the block’s slot. Method: skill l1-document-ingestion, “Summarising prose blocks”.ADVISORY, never a gate: this step does not hold up Task_Citeable, and check:l1-complete reports the backlog (block-summaries) without failing on it. Confirming or rejecting a draft is a person’s act, in bun run cat narratives. | . | Record errata in the source’s own textTask_Errata | Ingestion Engine (agent, runs unattended) | l1-document-ingestion | Owner, 2026-11-11 (who-iris, card Q-ODD-1 = A, and “add to L1 doc schema errata”). Reading the blocks to summarise them finds errors that are in the publication itself, not in the extraction: a title that says June 2006 over an introduction that says June 2005, a Spanish edition announcing nine recommendations where the English lists ten. The block stays as printed. The agent records an erratum in library/<bib-slug>/errata.json (folio-document-errata/v1): the kind, the block or page, the words as printed, the reading the evidence supports, the evidence, and its note as a draft narrative a person confirms in bun run cat narratives. An extraction defect is not an erratum: it is fixed by re-deriving the entry. ADVISORY: check:l1-complete reports errata and fails only on a file that does not mean what it says. Method: skill l1-document-ingestion, “Errata: errors in the source’s own text”. | . | Available to cite as an L1 sourceTask_Citeable | Ingestion Engine (agent, runs unattended) | document-intake | Every knowledge-graph reference to this source now resolves through library/. Authoring and review consume it from here – see authoring-a-document.bpmn. | .

6f7d60525212.doc: L1 document ingestion — a document to the L1 source knowledge graph
6f7d60525212.title: Decisions
6f7d60525212.content: Every one of the 3 decision(s) is documented. | decision | what decides it | branches | . | A theme source? (author’s judgement)Gateway_ThemeSource | Human or agentic judgement at the gateway, not a declared predicate. THE PREDICATE IS DELIBERATELY ABSENT: no testable rule (a captured web deployment, or a document that STATES palette and typography rules) decides it, because whether a source is a theme is an authoring decision.So this gateway is answered by whoever is ingesting, not computed. An arbitrary branded PDF is not a theme source because a rule says so; it is not one because the author says it is not.WHY IT IS A GATEWAY AND NOT A FILTER INSIDE THE SUBPROCESS. ingest-theme.bpmn starts at “Theme source in hand” and can refuse as incomplete. Routing every document into it would make “this is not a theme” and “this theme is malformed” the same refusal, and the second is a defect while the first is the normal case. | yes → Ingest the themeno → Build the L1 knowledge graph | . | Bean claimed?GW_BeanYours | Reads which end Process_BeanOpen reached. claimed: the bean is in progress and this process works it. not yours: a sibling session or a human holds it, nothing was written to it, and this process stops here rather than work a bean it does not own (bean-coordination). | claimed → Basic ingestion (harness)not yours → Not yours — left alone | . | L1 complete?Gateway_Complete | The verdict of the L1 completeness gate. gap records the gap as a bean; complete promotes the source into library/<bib-slug>/. | gap → Record the gap as a beancomplete → Move into library// | .

faed85a6f685.title: L2 component edit and review
faed85a6f685.content: Process_L2ComponentEditReview · advisory · 6 step(s) . One pass over one L2 DAK component: the agent edits it, runs its checker, renders and stages it with a before/after, and hands it on; review forks off beside the hand-on and never holds it up (adjudication is QA, not a gate). Called once per component pass by each authoring track of l2-dak-authoring.bpmn (Process_L2Dak). Only the call’s inputs differ between components (skill l2-component-edit-review, “The inputs, per component”): . | component: personas and user scenarios (C2, C3), business processes (C4), core data elements and glossary (C5) with their terminology bindings, decision-support and scheduling logic (C6, C7), indicators and requirements (C8, C9); | authoring skill: l2-dak-authoring, bpmn-authoring, dmn-authoring or terminology-management, named on the calling activity, so it joins this process’s skills along the call path (review-task.bpmn’s scoped composition); | renderer and diff: what the reviewer sees, before and after; | checker: the mechanical checks the agent runs before asking anyone; | reviewing role: the person who takes this process’s reviewer lane for the call. | . i i i i i i

8cf36a7ab7c6.title: Steps
8cf36a7ab7c6.content: Every one of the 6 step(s) is documented. | step | lane | skill / sub-process | what it does | . | Edit the componentTask_Edit | Authoring agent | l2-component-edit-review | Create or change the component with the authoring skill the call names, one component per pass. On rework, apply the review’s findings; a fix written in an AuditNote is applied as given. An adapted component is edited against its pinned upstream, so the before side of the diff is that upstream, not an empty file. | . | Run the component’s checkerTask_Check | Authoring agent | content-validatecontent-testartefact-reachability | The mechanical checks for this component, before anyone is asked (skill l2-component-edit-review, column “checker”): BPMN imports in bpmn-js with no warnings and its lanes map to personas (dak-swimlanes.ts); DMN loads, its decisions are reachable (artefact-reachability, audit:reachability) and its test cases run (content-test); the data dictionary web annex’s ids are unique and its references and terminology bindings resolve (check-web-annexes.ts); personas, scenarios and requirements each trace to an L1 recommendation (recommendation-extraction’s implementedBy edges). Findings go with the review request; a failing check does not stop the hand-on. | . | Render, stage, before/afterTask_RenderStage | Authoring agent | before-after-previewfeature-staging | Render the component the way its reviewer reads it (column “renderer and diff”): the BPMN diagram (render:bpmn) with a visual-diff picture; the DMN decision table (smart-base-transform.py dmn2html) with each rule’s L1 citation; the data dictionary’s term diff (dak-data-dictionary-diff.ts) and the chosen wireframe of each form; personas, scenarios and requirements as a prose diff. Commit to the feature branch so it is staged as branches/<slug>/ on the platform’s just-the-docs site (for smart-base, a folio-assistant staging re-pin, never the IG’s /deploy), and make the before/after preview here so it exists when review starts. | . | Ask for review with staging deep linksTask_RequestReview | Authoring agent | staging-reviewinteraction-modality | Ask the person in the reviewing role, following staging-review’s deep-link rule: one deep link per changed page and anchor on branches/<slug>/, each beside the same page on main (or “new page”), the pages taken from the change (rendered-impact); say so if there is no preview yet. Lead with what changed in prose, then the links, the before/after and the checker’s findings; put the question in interaction-modality’s form. Post it where the work is discussed (this conversation, the originating GitHub issue, the pull request), with the same links in each. A comment tagged on the PR becomes a review-comment todo (review-comments). | . | Review the staged componentCall_Review | Component reviewer (person) | calls Review taskcontent-reviewvisual-diffl2-component-edit-review | cat-harness’s generic review, called: classify what changed, review it, and record a qa-review/v1 QaReview whose subject is the component and whose Decision carries the reviewing role. The reviewer reads the staged page and the before/after; for a figure or table, the visual-diff picture and its changed-pixel count; for a form, the wireframe (wireframe-design-review; at L3 its Questionnaire follows fhir-questionnaire-wireframe). What to judge per component is in the skill’s column “the reviewer judges”. | . | Reopen upstream, flag derived assetsTask_ReopenUpstream | Authoring agent | todo-managerl2-component-edit-review | File a bean against the stage that chose the rejected source or dependency (check for an existing one first), and mark every asset derived from this component adjudication: rejected-upstream on its wasDerivedFrom edge. Nothing is deleted: the re-derivation may come out the same. | .

f483a1286976.content: Every one of the 15 step(s) is documented. | step | lane | skill / sub-process | what it does | . | Scope the DAKTask_ScopeDak | Programme manager / technical officer | content-plan | Enumerate the processes, decisions and data elements the guideline implies; identify the actors. | . | Build the L1 library from Component 1Task_L1Library | Business analyst | dak-l1-library | Ingest the DAK into the library; it is L2, so it gets no L1 graph. Record on its intake whether each is L1 (declared > context > inferred; –record-context writes §1.2’s context). For each L1 source, run l1-specialise.ts: its publication, sections and elements as specialisations of its library nodes, since the library is upstream of L1. 76805839411b.title: Publish a folio’s Lean render with the harness chrome
76805839411b.content: Process_LeanDocsPublish · strict · 2 step(s) . Build the visualiser of a folio’s declared lean directory — the Lake package’s doc-gen4 HTML render — and put it inside the folio’s built site with the harness navbar and rail. Two steps in two lanes. The build is a Lake run over the folio’s warm olean cache: expensive, and able to damage the cache (a Lake build over an untraced restore evicts it), so it sits with the Lean toolchain and refuses rather than risks. The publish is a file pass over the build’s output that cannot touch the cache; it sits with the build pipeline, after the site is built and before the chrome check and deploy, where stage-folio-local.ts rails the folio’s own pages. Only End_Ready publishes: a refused guard, a failed build and an unrailed page are each reported as such, never as a complete site without Lean docs. i i

88ef15c64be2.title: Logging what you are doing
88ef15c64be2.content: Skill log-message: Say what you are doing, to the Logger, in a form a reader can act on. Five required fields and one optional body; an incomplete message is not logged. Callable from any task in any process, and required by some. Named by: Complete initialization, Determine the harness and repositories, Initialize a harness, Log a message . You are the author of a log line; the Logger is where it goes. The Logger records and decides nothing, so it cannot know who acted: you supply actor. It is carried out as a sub-process: nobody starts there. A task in another process calls it, and the calling task’s diagram says so; this skill does not list its callers or the process that implements it.

fdb9d11fddd3.title: The message
fdb9d11fddd3.content: Five strings, all required, and one optional markdown body. | field | what it answers | shape | . | timestamp | when | an ISO-8601 instant, e.g. 2026-09-20T14:03:11Z | . | actor | who was acting | the acting actor’s id — never the Logger’s | . | process | inside which process | a process id, e.g. my-process | . | task | at which step of it | a node id within that process, e.g. A_DoTheThing | . | message | what happened | one line, no newline | . | body | the detail, if any | markdown, optional | . All five are required: each answers a question a reader would otherwise guess. body is the one place free prose belongs. A diff, an error, the contents of a file that was not where it should have been. Keep message to the line somebody scanning will read, and put everything else here.

0fa5c2e9ff5c.title: When to log
0fa5c2e9ff5c.content: Optionally, from any task in any process. You need no permission and no element in the diagram: an actor saying what it is doing is always in order. Required where a diagram says so, which it says by drawing the call explicitly — a callActivity whose calledElement is Process_LogMessage. If the diagram drew it, logging is a step, not a courtesy. The difference between the two is only whether the caller drew it. It is the same sub-process either way, and it takes the same six fields.

42e05d8820d5.title: If you cannot complete the message
42e05d8820d5.content: Do not log, and say that you could not. The End_NotLogged branch is a real outcome, not an error path to route around. A line missing its actor or its task still looks like a record, and a reader cannot tell it from a complete one. The same holds if the Logger is unreachable: say so, in the place you would have logged to, and carry on with the task. Logging is not a gate. A failure to log is never a reason to abandon an install.

76297772f39e.title: The one destination bootstrap has
76297772f39e.content: The discussion with the human actor. A Bootstrapping Agent has no log file, no service and no work plan — the only place it can put a line where a person will see it is the conversation it is already in. There is no command: the agent writes the six fields into the conversation. A harness that installs a real log sink adds a Tool for it; this skill still says what a message is.

7862739825a1.title: What this skill is NOT
7862739825a1.content: A log line says what an actor did at a moment; it is not a record of work still outstanding. Logging is also not asking: if a step needs a judgement, that is confirm-harness, and no number of log lines substitutes for it.

be0eed9b1c41.title: The Logger’s contract
be0eed9b1c41.content: Skill logger: The contract a Logger keeps: accept a complete log message, record it unchanged where a person can read it, attributed to the actor the message names. A mechanical Actor plays this Role; this is what it must do, and what it can be tested against. Named by: Log a message . A Logger plays a Role, and this is the Role’s contract. The author of a log line follows log-message. This skill is the other side: what happens to the line once it arrives. It sits in the Logger lane of log-message.

f309b345806f.title: Responsibilities
f309b345806f.content: . | Record a complete message unchanged. All five fields log-message requires (timestamp, actor, process, task, message), and body when given, are recorded as received. No field is rewritten, truncated or filled in. | Attribute it to the actor the message names. The line says the actor field’s value acted. It never names the Logger. | Put it where a person can read it. In bootstrap that is the discussion the human actor is already in. A harness that installs a log sink adds a Tool for it, and this contract still holds. | Say when it cannot record. If the destination is unreachable, the failure is reported to the author, so log-message’s “say that you could not” can happen. A message is never dropped silently. | .

116efe44fcd0.title: Tests
116efe44fcd0.content: Bootstrap runs nothing, so the test named in tested-by: lives with the toolset. It checks line 1 (the fields match log-message, and only a complete message reaches the Logger lane). Lines 2–4 concern the destination, the discussion, and are not tested.

f62231f7c1ab.title: Not its responsibility
f62231f7c1ab.content: Composing the message, judging whether it is complete, or deciding what happens next. Those happen in the acting Actor’s lane before anything reaches the Logger.

51b8d26c6e73.title: Managing agent context
51b8d26c6e73.content: TR… . On this page . | Three things that share the word overlay | What a Context Overlay is | What the Context layer holds | Why overlaying makes a test repeatable | Where the rules live | . This page is generated from docs/source/guides-managing-agent-context/ — each section below links to its own source. ✎ Edit QA… TR… . An agent does not arrive at a task knowing nothing. It arrives carrying directives, memories, a record of how this person wants to be asked, and whatever confirmations were granted in advance. All of that is context: it shapes how a process runs without being part of what the process produces. A Context Overlay is a set of that material applied deliberately, so the same workflow can be run again under the same conditions — or run twice under deliberately different ones, and the difference attributed to the context rather than to chance.

189024a442c0.title: Three things that share the word overlay
189024a442c0.content: ✎ Edit QA… TR… . “Overlay” means three unrelated things in this documentation, so the Term on this page is Context Overlay and not the bare word. | where | what it means | . | this page | a set of context material applied to a run | . | getting-started §6 | a BRANCH of the folio-intent gateway — converting a repository you already have | . | getting-started §8 | positioning text ON cat artwork, where an undeclared region means “do not overlay” | . A reader who carries the bare word’s meaning from one section into another is misled in a way that is hard to notice, because every sentence still parses. So: Context Overlay when this page’s sense is meant. Where the other two are meant, name them — the gateway branch, or the art region.

86b9339c613c.title: What a Context Overlay is
86b9339c613c.content: ✎ Edit QA… TR… . Context is generated in several different ways, and the point of the Term is that they compose. A Context Overlay MAY be assembled from any of them: . | Agent directives — the instruction files an agent reads on arrival. | Memory — durable facts an agent carries between sessions. | Interaction preferences — how this person wants to be asked. | Waivers — confirmations granted in advance, each naming one gate. | Methodologies — an adopted way of reaching a judgement. | . What makes them one kind of thing is not their format. It is their relation to a running process: . Context is READ during a process and never written by one. The graph layer checks it. A step that writes to a Context graph is a defect, not an update — which is exactly what makes an overlay reproducible: if a run could modify its own context, the second run would not be the same experiment.

6994db376241.title: What the Context layer holds
6994db376241.content: ✎ Edit QA… TR… . The Context layer is declared, not inferred. Five graph typologies currently sit in it, and the schema requires each kind to say which layer it belongs to, so a kind that has not decided does not compile: . | kind | what it holds | . | memory | durable facts an agent carries between sessions | . | interaction | how a person wants to be asked — read at session start | . | waiver | confirmations granted in advance, each naming one gate | . | methodology | an adopted way of reaching a judgement, kept whole | . | fsh-guts | deprecated and throwaway structured content, kept addressable | . Ask the code rather than this table — graphTypologiesOfLayer("context") returns the live answer; a count written into prose is not re-derived. The shapes are in schemas/cat-harness.ts. fsh-guts holds structured material that COULD be rendered, which is what makes it look like content. It is context because no running process writes it.

0ba5e78ffb8e.title: Why overlaying makes a test repeatable
0ba5e78ffb8e.content: ✎ Edit QA… TR… . The reason to name this at all is testing. If context is ambient — whatever happened to be in the environment when the run started — then two runs of the same workflow are not comparable, and a difference in outcome cannot be attributed. Was it the model? The prompt? A memory entry one session wrote and another did not have? . Overlaying context makes that question answerable. The workflow is held fixed, the Context Overlay is stated, and a difference between runs is a difference between overlays. It is the same move as pinning a dependency version, because an unpinned one makes every other measurement unreliable. This is what lets the repository ask how models compare across sub-workflows under a controlled overlay of context and memories — a question named as open research in agentic-harness, not as something settled here.

ae95428f4e06.title: Where the rules live
ae95428f4e06.content: ✎ Edit QA… TR… . This page explains the concept. The discipline is in the skills, and where the two disagree the skill wins: . | agent-memory — the three entry labels, why entries are authored as nodes rather than in the generated file, and the injection budget. | content-context-and-state-graphs — the one question that settles a layer, and why a step writing to a Context graph is a defect. | confirmation-waiver — a confirmation granted in advance, scoped to a session or a process run. | interaction-modality — how a person wants to be asked. | . Setting an agent’s context deterministically from the knowledge graph at each task is not yet built. It is said here because a page that described it as working would read exactly like one that described something real.

6ca8cc2cdb30.title: Materialize remote content: the shared subprocess
6ca8cc2cdb30.content: Process_MaterializeRemote · strict · 7 step(s) . One process, called wherever remote content is landed locally: a large remote collection with no restrictions known in context may be materialized locally, size permitting, and bootstrapping a harness is the same shape. Two callers today and they are genuinely the same shape: sample-import.bpmn landing three items out of an ~0.7 TB catalogue, and bootstrap fetching a harness. upstream-pins.json is half of the second one’s refresh and names itself neither. STRICT, and the five gates are why. Each is a decision a person makes and none is answerable from a file, so a gate that only warned would be a gate nobody fails. The three states (referenced / materialized / unknown) and the five gates are schemas/materialization.ts in folio-assistant-core. Nothing here restates them. i i i i i i i
